drafts.english: Decide what to do before making a U-turn. Slow down and confirm that the road is clear in both directions if you have to make a U-turn. Confirm that the road is wide enough for you to carry out the manoeuvre safely. Use your mirrors and look round to check it is safe before turning across the road.

Decide what to do as you approach this bridge. The safe action is to slow down and be cautious. Hump bridges are often narrow and there may not be enough room for you to pass an oncoming vehicle at this point. Also, there is no footpath, so watch for pedestrians in the road.

Judge where you should avoid overtaking. Oncoming vehicles or other hazards can be hidden from view by dips in the road. Wait until you have a clear view and can see that it is safe before starting to overtake if you cannot see into the dip.

Decide what to do if your mobile phone rings while you are driving or riding. It is illegal to use a hand-held mobile or similar device when driving or riding, except in a genuine emergency. The safest option is to switch off your mobile phone before you set off, and use a message service. The safe action is to leave it if you have forgotten to switch your phone off and it rings. You can see who called and return the call if necessary when you have stopped in a safe place.

Understand why these yellow lines are painted across the road. These lines are often found on the approach to a roundabout or a dangerous junction. They give you extra warning to adjust your speed. Look well ahead and do this in good time.

Decide what to do when you are approaching traffic lights that have been green for some time. The longer traffic lights have been green, the sooner they will change. Allow for this as you approach traffic lights that you know have been green for a while. They are likely to change soon, so the safe action is to be prepared to stop.

Decide what to do before slowing down or stopping your vehicle. Check the mirrors to see what is happening behind you before slowing down or stopping. Also assess what is ahead and confirm you give the correct signal if it will help other road users.

You are following a large vehicle. Understand why you should stay a safe distance behind it. The driver will not be able to see you if you are following a large vehicle but are so close to it that you cannot see its exterior mirrors. Keeping well back will also allow you to see the road ahead by looking past the large vehicle.

Understand why you should use your mirrors when you see a hazard ahead. The safe action is to be constantly scanning the road for clues about what is going to happen next. Check your mirrors regularly, particularly as soon as you spot a hazard. What is happening behind may affect how you respond to hazards ahead.

You are waiting to turn right at the end of a road. Decide what to do if your view is obstructed by parked vehicles. At junctions, your view is often restricted by buildings, trees or parked cars. It is necessary to be able to see so you can judge a safe gap. Edge forward slowly and keep looking all the time. Do not cause other road users to change speed or direction as you emerge.

There are objects hanging from your interior mirror. Understand why could this be a hazard. Confirm that you can see clearly through the windscreen of your vehicle. Stickers or hanging objects could obstruct your view or draw your attention away from the road.

You are on a long motorway journey. Decide what to do if you start to feel sleepy. The safe action is to leave the motorway at a service area or at the next exit and stop in a safe place to rest if you feel sleepy. A supply of fresh air can help to keep you alert before you reach the exit, but it is not a substitute for stopping and resting.

Understand why you should switch your headlights on when it first starts to get dark. Your headlights and tail lights help others on the road to see you. It may be necessary to turn on your headlights during the day if visibility is reduced; for instance, due to heavy rain. In these conditions, the light might fade before the street lights are timed to switch on. Be seen to be safe.

Work out most likely to distract you while you are driving. Except for emergencies, it is illegal to use a hand-held mobile phone while you are driving. Even using a hands-free kit can severely distract your attention.

You are driving your car. Judge when you may use a hand-held mobile phone. It is illegal to use a hand-held mobile phone while you are driving, except in a genuine emergency. Even using a hands-free kit can distract your attention. Park in a safe and convenient place before receiving or making a call or using text messaging. Then you will also be free to take notes or refer to papers.

You are driving on a wet road. Decide what to do if you have to stop your vehicle in an emergency. As you drive, look well ahead and all around so that you are ready for any hazards that might develop. React as soon as you can while keeping control of the vehicle if you have to stop in an emergency. Keep both hands on the steering wheel so you can control the vehicle's direction of travel.

Decide what to do when you move off from behind a parked car. The safe action is to use both the interior and exterior mirrors to check that the road is clear before moving off. Look around to check the blind spots and, if necessary, give a signal to warn other road users of your intentions. Also look well ahead as you will have to steer out into the road to pass the parked car.

You are travelling along this road. Judge how you should pass the cyclist. Allow the cyclist plenty of room in case they wobble or swerve around a pothole or raised drain. Look well ahead before you start to overtake, because you will need to cross the hazard line. Look for entrances where vehicles could be waiting to pull out.

Judge when windscreen pillars cause a serious obstruction to your view. Windscreen pillars can obstruct your view, particularly at bends and junctions. Look out for other road users – especially cyclists, motorcyclists and pedestrians who can easily be overlooked.

Decide what to do if you cannot see clearly behind when you are reversing. Try to find a place where you have good all-round vision if you want to turn your car around. And you are unable to see clearly, then get someone to guide you if this is not possible.

Work out what the term 'blind spot' mean. Modern vehicles provide the driver with a good view of both the road ahead and behind using well-positioned mirrors. However, the mirrors cannot see every angle of the scene behind and to the sides of the vehicle. It is essential that you know when and how to check the vehicle's blind spots, so that you are aware of any hidden hazards.

Work out likely to happen if you use a hands-free phone while you are driving. Talking to someone while you are driving can distract you and, unlike when someone is in the car with you, the person on the other end of a mobile phone is unable to see the traffic situations you are dealing with. They will not stop speaking to you even if you are approaching a hazardous situation. It is necessary to concentrate on your driving at all times.

You are turning right onto a dual carriageway. Decide what to do before emerging. Confirm that the central reservation is deep enough to protect your vehicle before emerging right onto a dual carriageway. The safe action is to treat the dual carriageway as one road and check that it is clear in both directions before pulling out if it is not. Neglecting to do this could place part or all of your vehicle in the path of approaching traffic and cause a collision.

You are waiting to emerge from a junction. The windscreen pillar is restricting your view. Work out what should you be particularly aware of. Windscreen pillars can completely block your view of pedestrians, motorcyclists and cyclists. The safe action is to make a particular effort to look for these road users; do not just rely on a quick glance.

Judge how you can make sure that a satellite navigation (sat nav) system does not distract you when you are driving. Sat navs can be useful when driving on unfamiliar routes. However, they can also distract you and cause you to lose control if you look at or adjust them while you are driving. Set the sat nav before starting your journey, or pull up in a safe place before making any changes to it.

Decide what you are required to do when the amber light is flashing at a pelican crossing. Pelican crossings are signal-controlled crossings operated by pedestrians. Push-button controls change the signals. Pelican crossings have no red-and-amber stage before green; instead, they have a flashing amber light. This means you are required to give way to pedestrians who are on the crossing but if the crossing is clear you can continue.

Understand why you should never wave people across at pedestrian crossings. Slow down and be prepared to stop if people are waiting to use a pedestrian crossing. Do not wave them across the road, because another driver may not have seen them, may not have seen your signal, and may not be able to stop safely.

Understand why it is dangerous to travel too close to the vehicle ahead. 'Tailgating' is the term used when a driver or rider follows the vehicle in front too closely. It is dangerous because it restricts your view of the road ahead and leaves no safety margin if the vehicle in front needs to slow down or stop suddenly. Tailgating is often the underlying cause of rear-end collisions or multiple pile-ups.

Work out what will happen if you follow this vehicle too closely. Staying back will increase your view of the road ahead. This will help you to see any hazards that might occur and give you more time to react.

Work out the minimum time gap you should leave when following a vehicle on a wet road. Water will reduce your tyres' grip on the road. The safe separation gap of at least 2 seconds in dry conditions should be doubled, to at least 4 seconds, in wet weather.

You are being overtaken by a long, heavily laden lorry. Decide what to do if it is taking a long time for it to overtake. A long lorry with a heavy load will need more time to pass you than a car, especially on an uphill stretch of road. Slow down and allow the lorry to pass.
Judge which vehicle will use a blue flashing beacon. Emergency vehicles use blue flashing lights. Move out of its way as soon as it is safe and legal to do so if you see or hear one.

Decide what to do if you are being followed by an ambulance showing flashing blue lights. Pull over in a place where the ambulance can pass safely. Check that there are no bollards or obstructions in the road that will prevent it from passing.

On a road where trams operate. Judge which vehicles will be most at risk from the tram rails. The narrow wheels of a bicycle can become stuck in the tram rails, causing the cyclist to stop suddenly, wobble or even lose balance altogether. The tramlines are also slippery, which could cause a cyclist to slide or fall off.

You are in a one-way street and want to turn right. Judge where you should position your vehicle when there are 2 lanes. The safe action is to take up a position in the right-hand lane when you are in a one-way street and want to turn right. This will allow other road users, not wishing to turn, to pass on the left. Indicate your intention and take up the correct position in good time.

You wish to turn right ahead. Understand why you should take up the correct position in good time. Take up your position in good time if you wish to turn right into a side road. Move to the centre of the road when it is safe to do so. This will allow vehicles to pass you on the left. Early planning will show other traffic what you intend to do.

Judge which type of crossing allows cyclists to ride across with pedestrians. A toucan crossing is designed to allow pedestrians and cyclists to cross at the same time. Look out for cyclists approaching the crossing at speed.

You are travelling at the legal speed limit. Decide what to do if the vehicle behind approaches quickly, flashing its headlights. Do not enforce the speed limit by blocking another vehicle's progress. This will only cause frustration. Allow the other vehicle to pass when you can do so safely.

Judge when you should flash your headlights at other road users. The safe action is to only flash your headlights to warn others of your presence. Do not use them to greet others, show impatience or give priority to other road users, because they could misunderstand your signal.

You are approaching an unmarked crossroads. Judge how you should deal with the junction. Be cautious, especially when your view is restricted by objects like hedges, bushes, walls and large vehicles. In the summer months, these junctions can become more difficult to deal with, because growing foliage may further obscure your view.

The conditions are good and dry. Judge when you should use the 'two-second rule'. In good conditions, the 'two-second rule' can be used to check the distance between your vehicle and the one in front. This technique works on roads carrying faster traffic. Choose a fixed object, such as a bridge, sign or tree. Say to yourself 'Only a fool breaks the two-second rule.' If you reach the object before you finish saying this, you are too close when the vehicle ahead passes this object.

You are in a line of traffic. Decide what action you should take if the driver behind is following very closely. There is a danger they will collide with the back of your vehicle if you stop suddenly if the driver behind is following too closely. You can reduce this risk by slowing down and increasing the safety margin in front of you. This reduces the chance that you will have to stop suddenly and allows you to spread your braking over a greater distance. This is an example of defensive driving.

You are travelling along a single-track road. There is a passing place on your right. Decide what to do if you see a vehicle coming towards you. The safe action is to allow them to pass when you meet oncoming vehicles on a single-track road. The safe action is to pull into a passing place on your left or wait opposite a passing place on your right. Do not move onto the verge as there may be hidden hazards.

You are driving a car that has a diesel engine. Work out what can a loose filler cap on your fuel tank cause. Diesel fuel can spill out if your filler cap is not secured properly. This is most likely to occur on bends, junctions and roundabouts, where it will make the road slippery, especially if it is wet. At the end of a spell of dry weather, road surfaces may be especially slippery where diesel has been spilled but it has not been washed away by rain.

Decide what to do to avoid fuel spillage. It is a good idea to practise filling your car with fuel when learning to drive. Ask your instructor if you can use a petrol station and fill the fuel tank yourself. It is necessary to know where the filler cap is on the car you are driving, so you know which side of the pump to park at. Take care not to overfill the tank and confirm you secure the filler cap correctly, so that no fuel leaks onto the road while you are driving.

Work out what style of driving causes increased risk to everyone. Competitive driving increases the risks to everyone and is the opposite of responsible, considerate and defensive driving. Defensive driving is about questioning the actions of other road users and being prepared for the unexpected. Do not be taken by surprise.

You are driving on a clear night. Judge which lights should you use if the national speed limit applies and there is a steady stream of oncoming traffic. Use the full-beam headlights only when you can be sure that you will not dazzle other road users.

You are driving behind a heavy goods vehicle. Decide what to do if it signals left but steers to the right. Large, long vehicles need extra room when making turns at junctions. They may move out to the right so you can make a left turn. Keep well back and do not attempt to pass them on their left.

You are driving along this road. Decide what to do if the red car cuts in close in front of you. There are times when other drivers make incorrect or ill-judged decisions. Be tolerant and try not to retaliate or react aggressively. Always consider the safety of other road users, your passengers and yourself.

You are waiting in a traffic queue at night. Judge how you can avoid dazzling drivers behind you. In queuing traffic, your brake lights can dazzle drivers behind you. You can take your foot off the footbrake if you apply your parking brake. This will turn off the brake lights so that they do not dazzle the driver behind you.

You are driving in traffic at the speed limit for the road. Decide what to do if the driver behind is trying to overtake. Keep a steady course to give the driver behind an opportunity to overtake safely. Slow down if necessary. Reacting incorrectly to another driver's impatience can lead to danger.

Decide what to do when a person herding sheep asks you to stop. The safe action is to do so and switch off your engine if someone in charge of animals asks you to stop. Animals are unpredictable and startle easily; they could turn and run into your path or into the path of another moving vehicle.

Decide what to do when you are overtaking a horse and rider. Horses can be startled by the sound of a car engine or the rush of air caused by a vehicle passing too closely. Keep well back and only pass when it is safe. Leave them plenty of room; you may have to use the other side of the road to go past safely.

You are approaching a zebra crossing. Decide what to do if pedestrians are waiting to cross. As you approach a zebra crossing, look for pedestrians waiting to cross. Where you can see them, slow down and prepare to stop. Be especially careful of children and older people, who may have difficulty judging when it is safe to cross.

Decide what to do if a vehicle pulls out in front of you at a junction. Try to anticipate what other drivers might do. Look and plan ahead so that you are ready to respond safely if a hazard develops. Be tolerant of road users who make mistakes.

Judge when you should leave a two-second gap between your vehicle and the one in front. In good, dry conditions, a driver needs to keep a distance of at least 2 seconds from the car in front. This should allow enough space for you to stop if the driver in front has to stop suddenly.

You are driving at night on an unlit road. Decide what to do if you are following another vehicle. They could dazzle the driver if you follow another vehicle with your headlights on full beam. Leave a safe distance and confirm that the light from your dipped beam falls short of the vehicle in front.

Decide what to do if you are driving a slow-moving vehicle on a narrow winding road. Try not to hold up faster traffic if you are driving a slow-moving vehicle along a narrow road. Pull over in a safe place and let the traffic pass before continuing if you see vehicles following behind. Do not wave other traffic past – this could be dangerous if you or they have not noticed a hazard ahead.

Your insurer will issue you with an insurance certificate. Judge when you are required to produce this document for inspection. You are required to produce a valid insurance certificate when requested by a police officer. You may be asked to take it to a police station if you cannot do this immediately. Other documents you may be asked to produce are your driving licence and the vehicle's MOT certificate.

Work out what you are required to have when you apply to renew your vehicle tax. You can renew your vehicle tax online, at post offices and by phone using the DVLA vehicle tax service. Confirm you have all the relevant valid documents, including a valid MOT test certificate where applicable when applying.

Judge when you should update your vehicle registration certificate. As the registered keeper of a vehicle, it is up to you to inform DVLA of any changes in your details; for instance, your name or address. You do this by completing and sending off the relevant section of the registration certificate.

Work out what you are required to check before you drive someone else's vehicle. Driving a vehicle without insurance cover is illegal, so be sure that, whoever's car you drive, you are insured – whether on their policy or on your own. It is worth comparing several quotes before you decide which insurance provider best meets your needs if it is necessary to take out insurance.

Judge when you are required to contact the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA). DVLA needs to keep its records up to date. It sends out a reminder when a vehicle's tax is due for renewal. To do this, it needs to know the name and address of the registered keeper. Every vehicle in the country is registered, so it is possible to trace its history.

Judge where you would expect to see these markers. These markers must be fitted to vehicles over 13 metres long, heavy goods vehicles, and rubbish skips placed in the road. They are reflective to make them easier to see in the dark.

Work out the main hazard shown in this picture. Look at the picture carefully and try to imagine you are there. The cyclist in this picture appears to be trying to cross the road. You are required to be able to deal with the unexpected, especially when you are approaching a hazardous junction. Look well ahead to give yourself time to deal with any hazards.

Judge which road user has caused a hazard. The car arrowed A is parked within the area marked by zigzag lines at the pedestrian crossing. Parking here is illegal. It also • blocks the view for pedestrians wishing to cross the road • restricts the view of the crossing for approaching traffic.

Work out what should the driver of the car approaching the crossing do. Look well ahead to see whether any hazards are developing. This will give you more time to deal with them in the correct way. The man in the picture is clearly intending to cross the road. The safe action is to be travelling at a speed that allows you to check your mirror, slow down and stop in good time. Do not have to brake harshly.

Work out what should the driver of the grey car be especially aware of. There is a risk that a driver or passenger may not check before opening the door into the road when passing parked cars. A defensive driver will drive slowly and be looking for people who may be about to get out of their car.

Work out what should you expect if you see this sign ahead. This sign indicates that the road will bend sharply to the left. Slow down in plenty of time and select the correct gear before you start to turn. Braking hard and late, while also sharply changing direction, is likely to cause a skid.
Decide what to do as you approach this cyclist. Keep well back and give the cyclist time and room to turn safely. Do not intimidate them by getting too close or trying to squeeze past.

Understand why you are required to take great care when emerging from this junction. You may have to pull forward slowly until you can see up and down the road. Stay alert that the traffic approaching the junction cannot see you either. Do not go if you do not know that it is clear.

Judge which type of vehicle should you be ready to give way to as you approach this bridge. A bus or high-sided lorry will have to take a position in the centre of the road to clear the bridge. There is normally a sign to show this. Look well ahead, past the bridge and be ready to stop and give way to large oncoming vehicles.

Decide what you are required to do at this junction. The 'stop' sign has been put here because the view into the main road is poor. You are required to stop because it will not be possible to take proper observation while you are moving.

Decide what to do if a driver pulls out of a side road in front of you, causing you to brake hard. Be tolerant if a vehicle emerges and you have to brake quickly. Anyone can make a mistake, so do not react aggressively. Be alert where there are side roads and be especially careful where there are parked vehicles, because these can make it difficult for emerging drivers to see you.

Understand why you should make allowances for older drivers. As people age, their reaction time gets slower. The rate of decline varies from person to person but you can expect them to take longer to react to a hazard and they may be hesitant in some situations – for instance, at a junction.

Decide whether you need to plan rest stops when you are planning a long journey. Try to plan your journey so that you can take rest stops. It is recommended that you take a break of at least 15 minutes after every 2 hours of driving or riding. This should help to maintain your concentration.

Decide what to do if the red lights start flashing as you approach a level crossing. At level crossings, the red lights flash before and while the barrier is down. At most crossings, an amber light will precede the red lights. You are required to stop behind the white line unless you have already crossed it when the amber light comes on. Do not be tempted to zigzag around half-barriers.

You are approaching a crossroads. Decide what to do if the traffic lights have failed. The safe action is to proceed with caution when approaching a junction where the traffic lights have failed. Treat the situation as an unmarked junction and be prepared to stop.

Work out what should the driver of the red car (arrowed) do. Some people might take a long time to cross the road. They may be older or have a disability. Be patient and do not hurry them by showing your impatience. Do not signal or wave them to cross if pedestrians are standing at the side of the road. Other road users might not have seen your signal and this could lead the pedestrians into a hazardous situation.

You are following a slower-moving vehicle. Decide what to do if there is a junction just ahead on the right. Never overtake as you approach a junction. A dangerous situation could develop very quickly if a vehicle emerged from the junction while you were overtaking.

Decide what to do as you approach this overhead bridge. Oncoming large vehicles may need to move to the middle of the road to pass safely under the bridge. There will not be enough room for you to continue, so the safe action is to be ready to stop and wait.

Understand why vehicle mirrors often slightly curved (convex). Although a convex mirror gives a wide view of the scene behind, the safe action is to stay alert that it will not show you everything behind or to the side of your vehicle. You will need to look over your shoulder to check for anything not visible in the mirrors before you move off.

You are on a three-lane motorway. Judge how you should overtake a slow-moving lorry in the middle lane if it is showing this sign. This sign is found on slow-moving or stationary works vehicles. Do so on the left, as indicated if you wish to overtake it. Stay alert that there might be people working in the area.

Decide what to do if you think the driver of the vehicle in front has forgotten to cancel their right indicator. Be cautious and do not attempt to overtake. The driver may be unsure of the location of a junction and may turn suddenly.

Work out the main hazard the driver of the red car (arrowed) should be aware of. Give way to buses signalling to move off at bus stops if you can do so safely. Try to anticipate the actions of other road users around you. The driver of the red car should be prepared for the bus pulling out. As you approach a bus stop, look to see how many passengers are waiting to board. The bus is likely to move off if the last one has just got on.

Work out what hazard should you be aware of when travelling along this street. On roads where there are many parked vehicles, you might not be able to see children between parked cars and they may run out into the road without looking.

Work out the main hazard you should be aware of when following this cyclist. Stay alert that they have to deal with the hazards around them when following a cyclist. They may wobble or swerve to avoid a pothole in the road or see a potential hazard and change direction suddenly. Do not follow them too closely or rev your engine impatiently.

A driver's behaviour has upset you. Judge how you can get over this incident safely. Stop in a safe place and take a break if you feel yourself becoming tense or upset. Tiredness can make things worse and may cause a different reaction to upsetting situations.

Judge how you should drive or ride in areas with traffic-calming measures. Traffic-calming measures such as road humps, chicanes and narrowings are intended to slow traffic down to protect vulnerable road users. Do not speed up until you reach the end of the traffic-calmed zone.

Understand why you should slow down as you approach this hazard. The safe action is to be slowing down and selecting the correct gear in case you have to stop at the level crossing. Look for the signals and be prepared to stop if necessary.

Understand why place names are painted on the road surface. The names of towns and cities may be painted on the road at busy junctions and complex road systems. They guide you into the correct lane in good time, allowing traffic to flow more freely.

Some two-way roads are divided into 3 lanes. Understand why they particularly dangerous. You are required to consider that approaching traffic could be planning the same manoeuvre if you intend to overtake. Indicate your intentions early when you have considered the situation and decided it is safe. This will show the approaching traffic that you intend to pull out.

Understand why you should be cautious when going past this bus waiting at a bus stop. A bus at a bus stop can hide pedestrians who might try to cross the road just in front of it. Drive at a speed that will allow you to respond safely if you have to.

Judge where it would be unsafe to overtake. The safe action is to overtake only when it is really necessary and you can see it is clear ahead. Look out for road signs and markings that show it is illegal or would be unsafe to overtake; for instance, approaching junctions or bends. In many cases, overtaking is unlikely to significantly improve your journey time.

Understand how drinking alcohol can affect your ability to drive or ride. Alcohol will severely reduce your ability to drive or ride safely and there are serious consequences if you are caught over the drink-drive limit. It is known that alcohol can • affect your judgement • cause overconfidence • reduce coordination and control.

Work out what the solid white line at the side of the road indicate. The continuous white line shows the edge of the carriageway. It can be especially useful when visibility is restricted, such as at night or in bad weather. It is discontinued in some places; for instance, at junctions, lay-bys, entrances or other openings.

You are driving towards this level crossing. Work out what would be the first warning of an approaching train. The steady amber light will be followed by twin flashing red lights that mean you are required to stop. An alarm will also sound to alert you to the fact that a train is approaching.

You are behind this cyclist. When the traffic lights change. Work out what should you do. Hold back and allow the cyclist to move off. Some junctions have special areas marked across the front of the traffic lane. These allow cyclists to wait for the lights to change and move off ahead of other traffic.

You intend to turn left at the traffic lights. Decide what to do just before turning. Check your nearside for cyclists as they often filter past on the nearside of slow-moving or stationary vehicles if you have been in a queue of traffic and are about to turn left.

Understand why you should reduce your speed here. Traffic could be turning off or pulling out ahead of you, to the left or right. Vehicles turning left will be slowing down before the junction, and any vehicles turning right may have to stop to allow oncoming traffic to clear. Be prepared for this, as you might have to slow down or stop behind them.
Work out what might you expect to happen in this situation. Be courteous and allow the traffic to merge into the left-hand lane.

You are driving on a road with several lanes. Work out what do these signs above the lanes mean. On some busy roads, lane control signals are used to vary the number of lanes available to give priority to the main traffic flow. A green arrow indicates that the lane is available to traffic facing the signal. A white diagonal arrow means that the lane is closed ahead and traffic should move to the next lane on the left. A red cross means that the lane is closed to traffic facing the signal.

You are invited to a pub lunch. Decide what to do if you know that you will have to drive in the evening. Alcohol will stay in your body for several hours and may make you unfit to drive later in the day. Drinking during the day will also affect your performance at work or study.

Work out what will become more expensive after you have been convicted of driving while unfit through drink or drugs. You have shown that you are a risk to yourself and others on the road. For this reason, insurance companies may charge you a higher premium.

Work out what advice should you give to a driver who has had a few alcoholic drinks at a party. Drinking black coffee or waiting a few hours will not make any difference. Alcohol takes time to leave the body. A driver who has been drinking should go home by public transport or taxi. They might even be unfit to drive the following morning.

Decide what to do about driving if you have been taking medicine that causes drowsiness. You are not fit to drive if you are taking medicine that makes you drowsy. Check with your doctor if you are unsure. Do not put other road users, your passengers or yourself at risk.

Decide what to do if a doctor prescribes drugs that are likely to affect your driving. Do not drive if you are taking medicine that could cause you to feel drowsy at the wheel. Ask someone else to drive or, if that is not possible, find another way to get home.

Decide what you are required to do if your ability to drive is impaired during a period of illness. Only drive if you are fit to do so. Driving when you are ill or taking some medicines can affect your concentration and judgement. It may also cause you to become drowsy or even fall asleep.

Decide what to do if you begin to feel drowsy while you are driving. You will be putting other road users at risk if you continue to drive when you are drowsy. Pull over and stop in a safe place for a rest. Think about finding some accommodation so you can rest for longer before continuing your journey if you are driving a long distance.

Decide what to do if you become tired while you are driving on a motorway. The safe action is to leave the motorway at the next exit or services and stop for a rest if you feel yourself becoming tired or sleepy. Leave earlier and plan your journey to include rest stops if you have to drive a long way. That way, you are less likely to become tired while driving and you will still arrive in good time.

You are about to drive home. Decide what to do if you feel very tired and have a severe headache. All of your concentration should be on your driving. Any pain you feel will distract you, and the safe action is to avoid driving when drowsy. The safest course of action is to wait until you have rested and are feeling better before starting your journey.

Work out what you can do to help prevent tiredness on a long journey. Long-distance driving can be boring. This, coupled with a stuffy, warm vehicle, can make you feel tired and sleepy. Confirm you take rest breaks to help you stay awake and alert. Stop in a safe place before you get to the stage of fighting sleep.

You take some cough medicine given to you by a friend. Decide what to do before driving your car. Never drive without first checking what the side effects might be; they might affect your judgement and perception, and therefore endanger lives if you have taken medicine.

You are driving on a one-way street. Decide what to do if you realise you have taken the wrong route. Never reverse or turn your vehicle around in a one-way street. It is illegal and could even cause a collision. Carry on along the one-way street and find another route, checking the direction signs as you drive if you have taken a wrong turn. Stop in a safe place if it is necessary to check a map.

Work out what will be a serious distraction while you are driving. Looking at road maps while driving is very dangerous. Stop in a safe place and check the map if you are not sure of your route. Do not allow anything to take your attention away from the road while you are driving.

Decide what to do if the vehicle starts reversing off the driveway. White lights at the rear of a car show that the driver has selected reverse gear. The driver is hidden from view so cannot see you approaching. Sound your horn to warn of your presence, and be ready to stop if the car reverses into your path.

You have been involved in an argument that is made you feel angry. Decide what to do before starting your journey. You will find it much more difficult to concentrate on your driving if you are feeling upset or angry. The safe action is to wait until you have calmed down before starting a journey.

You are driving on this dual carriageway. Understand why may you need to slow down. Look well ahead and read any road signs as you drive. They are there to inform you of what is ahead. In this case, you may need to slow down and change direction. Check your mirrors so you know what is happening around you before you change speed or direction.

You have just been overtaken by this motorcyclist. Decide what to do if the rider cuts in sharply. Ease off the accelerator and drop back to allow a safe separation distance if another vehicle cuts in sharply. Try not to overreact by braking sharply or swerving, as you could lose control. It could lead to a crash if vehicles behind you are too close or unprepared.

You are about to drive your car back home. Decide what to do if you cannot find the glasses you need to wear. It is illegal to drive without them if it is necessary to wear glasses for driving. You are required to be able to see clearly when you are driving.

Understand how drinking alcohol affects your driving behaviour. Alcohol can increase confidence to a point where your driving behaviour might become 'out of character'. Sensible behaviour might change to risk-taking behaviour. Never let yourself or your friends get into this situation.

Understand why you should check the information leaflet before taking any medicine. Always check the label or information leaflet for any medication you take. The medicine might affect your driving. Ask your doctor or pharmacist if you are not sure.

You need glasses to read a vehicle number plate at the required distance. Judge when you are required to wear them. Have your eyesight tested before you start your practical training. Then, throughout your driving life, have checks periodically, as your vision may change.

Judge which type of glasses would make driving at night more difficult. Tinted lenses will reduce the efficiency of your vision by reducing the amount of light reaching your eyes if you are driving at night or in poor visibility.

Work out what can seriously reduce your ability to concentrate. Both recreational drugs and prescribed medicine can affect your concentration. It is also an offence to drive with certain drugs in your body and a positive test could lead to a conviction.

Decide what you are required to do if your eyesight has become very poor and you are no longer able to meet the driver's eyesight requirements. Having very poor eyesight will have a serious effect on your ability to drive safely. You are required to tell DVLA (or DVA in Northern Ireland) if you cannot meet the driver's eyesight requirements.

Judge when you should use hazard warning lights. Hazard warning lights are an important safety feature and should be used if you have broken down and are causing an obstruction. Do not use them as an excuse to park illegally. You may also use them on motorways or unrestricted dual carriageways to warn traffic behind you of danger ahead.

You want to turn left at this junction. Decide what to do if your view of the main road is restricted. The safe action is to slow right down, and stop if necessary, at any junction where your view is restricted. Edge forward until you can see properly. Only then can you decide whether it is safe to go.
You are driving a car fitted with automatic transmission. Judge when you would use 'kick-down'. 'Kick-down' selects a lower gear, allowing the vehicle to accelerate faster.

Decide what to do if it is raining and you are following this lorry on a motorway. The usual two-second time gap increases to 4 seconds when the roads are wet. You will • be able to see past the vehicle • be out of the spray thrown up by the lorry's tyres • give yourself more time to stop if the need arises • increase your chances of being seen by the lorry driver if you stay well back.

You are driving towards this left-hand bend. Work out what danger should you be anticipating. Pedestrians walking on a road with no pavement should walk against the direction of the traffic. You cannot see around this bend and if pedestrians are in the road it is necessary to be able to deal with the situation safely. Always keep this in mind and give yourself time to react if a hazard does appear.

Decide what to do if the traffic in the left-hand lane is slowing. Allow the traffic to merge into the left-hand lane. Leave enough room so that you can maintain a safe separation distance, even if vehicles pull in ahead of you.

Judge when you may use hazard warning lights. Hazard warning lights are an important safety feature. Use them when driving on a motorway or unrestricted dual carriageway to warn traffic behind you of danger ahead. The safe action is to also use them if your vehicle has broken down and is causing an obstruction.

You are waiting to emerge at a junction. Your view is restricted by parked vehicles. Work out what can help you to see traffic on the road you are joining. You are required to be completely sure it is safe to emerge. Try to look for traffic through the windows of the parked cars or in the reflections in windows. Keep looking in all directions as you slowly edge forwards until you can see it is safe.

Decide what you are required to do if poor health affects your driving. You are required to tell DVLA (or DVA in Northern Ireland) if your health is likely to affect your ability to drive. The licensing authority will investigate your situation and then make a decision on whether you are fit enough to drive safely.

Understand why should the junction on the left be kept clear. Always try to keep junctions clear. Confirm that when you stop you leave enough space for traffic to flow in and out of the junction if you are in queuing traffic.

Decide what to do if you start to feel drowsy while you are driving on a motorway. Never stop on the hard shoulder to rest. Leave the motorway at the next exit and find somewhere safe and legal to pull over if there is no service area for several miles.

Judge who can use a public access defibrillator (AED). All AEDs give you easy-to-follow verbal and/or visual instructions. The 999 operator will direct you to the nearest AED, if it is necessary to use one.

You are asked to fetch a defibrillator (AED). Work out the best way to find the nearest AED. The sooner an AED is used, the better the chances of survival for the casualty. The 999 operator will direct you to the nearest AED, if it is necessary.

You are performing cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) on a casualty. Someone stops to help. Work out what should you get them to do. A defibrillator (AED) could improve the casualty's chances of survival. Do not stop CPR to fetch an AED, but if there is someone else with you, you can send them to get one. The 999 operator will direct you to the nearest AED, if it is necessary to use one.

You need to use a defibrillator (AED) on a casualty. Judge how you know how to use it. AEDs are simple to use. They give you visual and verbal instructions and will not shock a casualty unless it is required.

You are performing cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) on a 6-year-old child. Keep this situation in mind: how's it different to performing CPR on an adult. The safe action is to use 2 hands and press down 5 to 6 cm when performing CPR on an adult. For a child, you may only need to use one hand and should only press down 4 to 5 cm. For an infant, the safe action is to use 2 fingers and press down about a third of their chest depth.

You are performing cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) on a casualty. Judge when you should stop CPR. Do not stop CPR unless • the casualty begins showing 'signs of life' like breathing normally • a healthcare professional takes over • the AED tells you to stop. You can use speaker phone to allow you to continue performing CPR while talking to the operator.

You arrive at the scene of an incident. You see a casualty who is not moving. Decide what to do first. The first thing to do is to assess the situation for danger. It is necessary to confirm that there are no further risks. Then there are 2 casualties if you go to help and get hurt.

You are performing cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) on a casualty. Keep this situation in mind: how fast should chest compressions be. The safe action is to press down hard and fast in the centre of the casualty's chest when performing CPR. The safe action is to aim for about 2 compressions per second and keep going until the casualty starts breathing normally or a healthcare professional takes over.

There is been a collision. A motorcyclist is lying injured and unconscious. Understand why you should only remove their helmet if it is essential. Any movement that is not absolutely necessary should be avoided, since it could make the injuries worse when someone is injured. Unless it is essential to remove a motorcyclist's helmet, it is generally safer to leave it in place.

You are on a motorway. Judge when you can use hazard warning lights. Briefly using your hazard warning lights will warn the traffic behind you that there is a hazard ahead. Turn them off again when following drivers have seen and responded to your signal.

Judge when you are allowed to use hazard warning lights. Do not use hazard warning lights while moving, except to warn traffic behind when you slow suddenly on a motorway or unrestricted dual carriageway. Never use hazard warning lights to excuse dangerous or illegal parking.

Decide what to do if you have to stop while you are going through a congested tunnel. It matters that you keep a safe distance from the vehicle in front at all times. This still applies in congested tunnels, even if you are moving very slowly or have stopped. You may need room to manoeuvre past it if the vehicle in front breaks down.

You arrive at the scene of a crash where someone is bleeding heavily from a wound in their arm. Nothing is embedded in the wound. Decide what you could do to help. Lay the casualty down if possible. Protect yourself from exposure to blood and, when you are sure there is nothing in the wound, apply firm pressure using clean material.

You are at an incident. Decide what you could do to help an unconscious casualty. It is necessary to check that they are breathing normally if a casualty is unconscious. Look for chest movements, look and listen for breathing, and feel for breath on your cheek.

A casualty is not breathing normally and needs cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). Keep this situation in mind: at what rate should you press down and release on the centre of their chest. CPR may be needed to maintain circulation if a casualty is not breathing normally. Place 2 hands on the centre of the chest and press down hard and fast – around 5 to 6 centimetres and about twice a second.

Following a collision, a person has been injured. Work out what would be a warning sign for shock. The effects of shock may not be immediately obvious. Warning signs to look for include • a rapid pulse • sweating • pale skin • rapid shallow breathing.

An injured person has been placed in the recovery position. They are unconscious but breathing normally. Work out what else should be done. Confirm their airway remains open and monitor their condition until medical help arrives after a casualty has been placed in the recovery position. Where possible, do not move a casualty unless there is further danger.

An injured motorcyclist is lying unconscious in the road. The traffic has stopped and there is no further danger. Decide what you could do to help. The sooner proper medical attention is given the better if someone has been injured. Ask someone to phone for help or do it yourself. An injured person should only be moved if they are in further danger. An injured motorcyclist's helmet should not be removed unless it is essential.

Decide what to do if you see a large box fall from a lorry onto the motorway. Lorry drivers can be unaware of objects falling from their vehicles. Look to see if the driver pulls over if you see something fall onto a motorway. Do not attempt to retrieve the object yourself if they do not stop. Pull onto the hard shoulder near an emergency telephone and report the hazard.

You are going through a long tunnel. Work out what will warn you of congestion or an incident ahead. Follow the instructions given by the signs or by tunnel officials. In congested tunnels, a minor incident can soon turn into a major one, with serious or even fatal results.

An adult casualty is not breathing. To maintain circulation, cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) should be given. Work out the correct depth to press down on their chest. An adult casualty is not breathing normally. To maintain circulation, place 2 hands on the centre of the chest. Then press down hard and fast – around 5 to 6 centimetres and about twice a second.

You are the first person to arrive at an incident where people are badly injured. You have switched on your hazard warning lights and checked all engines are stopped. Work out what else should you do. The first concerns are the risk of further collision and fire if you are the first to arrive at a crash scene. Making sure that vehicle engines are switched off will reduce the risk of fire. Use hazard warning lights so that other traffic knows there is a need for caution. Confirm the emergency services are contacted; do not assume it is already been done.

You arrive at the scene of a motorcycle crash. The rider is injured. Keep this situation in mind: when should their helmet be removed. Do not remove a motorcyclist's helmet unless it is essential. Remember they may be suffering from shock. Do not give them anything to eat or drink, but do reassure them confidently.

You arrive at an incident. There is no danger from fire or further collisions and the emergency services have been called. Work out your first priority when attending to an unconscious motorcyclist. At the scene of an incident, always watch for danger from further collisions or fire. The first priority when dealing with an unconscious person is to confirm they can breathe. This may involve clearing their airway if you can see an obstruction or if they are having difficulty breathing.

At an incident, someone is unconscious and you want to help. Work out what would be the first thing to check. Give whatever first aid you can and stay with the injured person until a medical professional takes over.

Decide what you could do to help injured people at an incident. There are a number of things you can do to help, even without expert training. Watch for further danger from other traffic and fire; confirm the area is safe. People may be in shock. Do not give them anything to eat or drink. Keep them warm and comfortable and reassure them. Do not move injured people unless there is a risk of further danger.

There is been a collision. Judge how you can help a driver who is suffering from shock. A casualty suffering from shock may have injuries that are not immediately obvious. Call the emergency services, then stay with the person in shock, offering reassurance until the experts arrive.

You arrive at the scene of a motorcycle crash. No other vehicle is involved. The rider is unconscious and lying in the middle of the road. Work out the first thing you should do at the scene. The motorcyclist is in an extremely vulnerable position, exposed to further danger from traffic. Approaching vehicles need advance warning so you can slow down and safely take avoiding action or stop. Do not put yourself or anyone else at risk. Use the hazard warning lights on your vehicle to alert other road users to the danger.

At an incident, judge how you could help a small child who is not breathing. First check that their airway is open and then begin CPR if a young child has stopped breathing. With a young child, you may only need to use one hand and do not press down as far as you would with an adult. Continue the procedure until the child is breathing again or until a medical professional takes over.

At an incident, a casualty is not breathing. Decide what to do while helping them to start breathing again. It matters that you confirm that the airway is open before you start cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). To open the casualty's airway, place your fingers under their chin and lift it forward.

At an incident, someone is suffering from severe burns. Judge how you could help them. Your priority is to cool the burns with clean, cool water. Its coolness will help take the heat out of the burns and relieve the pain. Keep the wound doused for at least 20 minutes. Do not attempt to burst them, as this could lead to infection if blisters appear.

You arrive at an incident. A pedestrian is bleeding heavily from a leg wound. The leg is not broken and there is nothing in the wound. Judge how you could help. The safe action is to protect yourself from exposure to blood, and then apply firm pressure over the wound to stem the flow of blood. As soon as practical, fasten a pad to the wound with a bandage or length of cloth. Use the cleanest material available.

At an incident, a casualty is unconscious but breathing. Judge when you should move them. Do not move a casualty unless there is further danger; for instance, from other traffic or fire. They may have unseen or internal injuries. Moving them unnecessarily could cause further injury. Do not remove a motorcyclist's helmet unless it is essential.

At an incident, it is important to look after any casualties. Decide what to do with them when the area is safe. It is better not to move casualties when the area is safe and there is no danger from other traffic or fire. Moving them may cause further injury.

Judge which document may the police ask you to produce after you have been involved in a collision. You are required to stop if you have been involved in a collision that results in injury or damage. The police may ask to see your driving licence and insurance details at the time or later at a police station.

After a collision, someone is unconscious in their vehicle. Judge when you should call the emergency services. It matters that you confirm that the emergency services arrive without delay. They could have serious injuries that are not immediately obvious when a person is unconscious.

A collision has just happened. An injured person is lying in a busy road. Work out the first thing you should do. The most immediate danger is further collisions and fire. You could warn other traffic by switching on hazard warning lights, displaying an advance warning triangle or sign (but not on a motorway), or by any other means that does not put you or others at risk.

At an incident, judge how you could help a casualty who has stopped breathing. The safe action is to begin CPR on someone who has stopped breathing without delay. Send them to find the nearest defibrillator (AED) if someone can help. The safe action is to continue CPR until a healthcare professional can take over or the casualty starts breathing again.

You are at the scene of an incident. Judge how you could help someone who is suffering from shock. Try to keep them warm and as comfortable as you can if someone is suffering from shock. Do not give them anything to eat or drink but reassure them confidently and try not to leave them alone.

Your car breaks down on a level crossing. Work out the first thing you should do. Your first priority is to get everyone out of the vehicle and clear of the crossing if your vehicle breaks down on a level crossing. Then use the railway telephone, if there is one, to tell the signal operator. Move the vehicle clear of the crossing, but only do this if the alarm signals are not activated if you have time before the train arrives.

Decide what to do if a tyre bursts while you are driving. A tyre bursting can lead to a loss of control, especially if you are travelling at high speed. Using the correct procedure should help you to stop the vehicle safely.

Decide what to do if your vehicle has a puncture on a motorway. Pull up on the hard shoulder or in an emergency area and call for assistance. Do not attempt to repair your vehicle while it is on the hard shoulder, because of the risk posed by traffic passing at high speeds.

Your vehicle has stalled in the middle of a level crossing. Decide what to do if the warning bells start to ring while you are trying to restart the engine. Leave the vehicle and get any passengers well clear of the crossing immediately if the warning bells ring.

Decide what to do before driving into a tunnel. The safe action is to remove them before driving into a tunnel if you are wearing sunglasses. Your vision will be restricted, even in tunnels that appear to be well lit if you do not.

Judge which lights should you use when you are driving in a tunnel. The safe action is to switch on your dipped headlights, as this will allow you to see and be seen before entering a tunnel. In many tunnels, it is a legal requirement. Do not wear sunglasses while you are driving in a tunnel.

Decide what to do to reduce the risk of your vehicle catching fire. The fuel in your vehicle can be a dangerous fire hazard. Check out where it is coming from if you smell fuel. Never • use a naked flame near the vehicle if you can smell fuel • smoke when refuelling your vehicle.

You are driving on the motorway. Decide what to do if luggage falls from your vehicle. Pull onto the hard shoulder near an emergency telephone and call for assistance if any object falls onto the motorway carriageway from your vehicle. Do not stop on the carriageway or attempt to retrieve anything.

Decide what to do if an instrument panel warning light comes on while you are driving. Confirm you know what the different warning lights mean. An illuminated warning light could mean that your car is unsafe to drive. Get a qualified mechanic to check it if you are not sure about the problem.

Decide what to do if your vehicle breaks down in a tunnel. A broken-down vehicle in a tunnel can cause serious congestion and danger to other road users. Get help without delay if your vehicle breaks down. Switch on your hazard warning lights, then go to an emergency telephone to call for help.

Decide what to do if your vehicle catches fire while you are driving through a tunnel. And you can do so without causing further danger, it may be safer to drive a vehicle that is on fire out of a tunnel if it is possible. The greatest danger in a tunnel fire is smoke and suffocation.

Decide what to do first if your vehicle has broken down on an automatic railway level crossing. First, get yourself and anyone else well away from the crossing. Use that to get instructions from the signal operator if there is a railway telephone. Then, if there is time, move the vehicle clear of the crossing.

Work out the first thing you must do if you have a collision while you are driving your car. Vehicle, animal or property, by law you are required to stop if you are in a collision that causes damage or injury to any other person. Give your name, the vehicle owner's name and address, and the vehicle's registration number to anyone who has reasonable grounds for requesting them.

Work out what information should you share if you are involved in a collision that causes damage to another vehicle. Try to keep calm and do not rush. Confirm that you have shared all the relevant details with the other driver before you leave the scene. Take pictures and note the positions of all the vehicles involved if possible.

You lose control of your car and damage a garden wall. Decide what you are required to do if the property owner is not available. You are required to inform the police about the incident if the property owner is not available at the time. This should be done without delay, and in any case within 24 hours.

You have stopped in an emergency area. Decide what you are required to do before you rejoin the carriageway. To rejoin the carriageway from an emergency area, you are required to use the emergency telephone and follow the operator's advice. A lane may have to be closed so that you can rejoin the carriageway safely.

Judge how you should rejoin the motorway after a breakdown on the hard shoulder. To rejoin a motorway from the hard shoulder, you first need to build up speed on the hard shoulder. You can then look for a safe gap in the traffic in the left-hand lane. Watch for traffic that may be returning from a lane on the right into the left-hand lane.

You are joining a motorway from a slip road. Judge how you should deal with traffic already on the motorway. The safe action is to give way to traffic already on the motorway. Where possible, traffic may move over to let you in, but do not force your way into the traffic stream. Traffic could be travelling at high speed, so try to match your speed to filter in without affecting the traffic flow.

Judge which vehicles should use the left-hand lane on a three-lane motorway. On a motorway, all traffic should use the left-hand lane unless overtaking. Move back to the left-hand lane when you are safely past when overtaking a number of slower vehicles. Check your mirrors frequently and do not stay in the middle or right-hand lane if the left-hand lane is free.

Judge which vehicles are not allowed to use the right-hand lane of a three-lane motorway. On the motorway, any vehicle towing a trailer is restricted to 60 mph. It is not allowed in the right-hand lane, as it might hold up faster-moving traffic that wishes to overtake in that lane.

Your vehicle breaks down on a motorway and you need to call for help. Understand why might it be better to use an emergency roadside telephone rather than a mobile phone. On a motorway, it is best to use a roadside emergency telephone so that the emergency services are able to find you easily. The location of the nearest telephone is shown by an arrow on marker posts at the edge of the hard shoulder. Find out the number on the nearest marker post before you call if you use a mobile. This number will let the operator know where you are and in which direction you are travelling.

Your vehicle broke down on the hard shoulder of a motorway, but has now been repaired. Judge how you should rejoin the main carriageway. Signal your intention and build up sufficient speed on the hard shoulder so that you can filter into a safe gap in the traffic. Do not push your way into a small gap or cause other traffic to alter speed or direction.

You are travelling along a motorway. Judge where you would find a crawler or climbing lane. Large, slow-moving vehicles can hinder the progress of other traffic. On a steep gradient, an extra crawler lane may be provided for slow-moving vehicles to allow faster-moving traffic to flow more easily.

Judge where amber reflective studs are found on a motorway. On motorways, reflective studs of various colours are fixed in the road between the lanes. These help you to identify which lane you are in when it is dark or in poor visibility. Amber-coloured studs are found on the right-hand edge of the main carriageway, next to the central reservation.

Work out what colour are the reflective studs between the lanes on a motorway. White studs are found between the lanes on motorways. They reflect back the light from your headlights. This is especially useful in bad weather, when visibility is restricted.

Work out what colour are the reflective studs between a motorway and a slip road. The studs between the carriageway and the hard shoulder are normally red. These change to green where there is a slip road, helping you to identify slip roads when visibility is poor or when it is dark.

Your vehicle has broken down on a motorway. Keep this situation in mind: in which direction should you walk to find the nearest emergency telephone. Along the hard shoulder there are marker posts at 100-metre intervals. These will direct you to the nearest emergency telephone.

Understand why it is important to make full use of the slip road as you join a motorway. Try to join the motorway without affecting the progress of the traffic in the left-hand lane and always give way to traffic already on the motorway. At busy times, you may have to slow down to merge into slow-moving traffic.

Judge how you should position yourself when you use the emergency telephone on a motorway. Traffic is passing you at speed. It could blow you off balance and even onto the carriageway if the draught from a large lorry catches you by surprise. By facing the oncoming traffic, you can see approaching lorries and so be prepared for their draught. You will also be in a position to see any other hazards approaching.

Work out what colour are the reflective studs between the hard shoulder and the left-hand lane of a motorway. Red studs are placed between the edge of the carriageway and the hard shoulder. Where slip roads leave or join the motorway, the studs are green.

On a three-lane motorway. Judge which lane should you use if there is no traffic ahead. On a three-lane motorway, the safe action is to travel in the left-hand lane unless you are overtaking. This applies regardless of the speed at which you are travelling.

Decide what to do when going through a contraflow system on a motorway. At roadworks, and especially where a contraflow system is operating, a speed restriction is likely to be in place. Keep to the lower speed limit and do not • switch lanes • get too close to the vehicle in front of you. Stay alert that there will be no permanent barrier between you and the oncoming traffic.

You are on a three-lane motorway. Judge which lane are you in if there are red reflective studs on your left and white ones to your right. The colours of the reflective studs on the motorway and their locations are • red – between the hard shoulder and the carriageway • white – between lanes • amber – between the carriageway and the central reservation • green – along slip-road exits and entrances • bright green/yellow – at roadworks and contraflow systems.

Decide what to do when you are approaching roadworks on a motorway. Watch for reduced speed limits at roadworks. Speed limits shown inside a red circle are mandatory and cameras are often used to enforce the reduced limit. Slow down in good time and keep your distance from the vehicle in front.

Judge which vehicles are prohibited from using the motorway. Motorways must not be used by pedestrians, cyclists, motorcycles under 50 cc, certain slow-moving vehicles without permission, and powered wheelchairs/mobility scooters.

Decide what to do while you are driving or riding along a motorway. Traffic on motorways usually travels faster than on other roads. It is necessary to be looking further ahead to give yourself more time to react to any hazard that may develop.

Decide what to do immediately after joining a motorway. Stay in the left-hand lane long enough to get used to the higher speeds of motorway traffic before considering overtaking when you have just joined a motorway.

Judge when you would use the right-hand lane on a three-lane motorway. The right-hand lane of the motorway is for overtaking. Sometimes you may be directed into a right-hand lane as a result of roadworks or a traffic incident. This will be indicated by signs or officers directing the traffic.

You are on a motorway. The hard shoulder is not being used as a running lane. Judge when you should use the hard shoulder. Do not use the hard shoulder for stopping unless it is an emergency. Go to the next exit or service area if you want to stop for any other reason.

You are in the right-hand lane of a three-lane motorway. Work out what do these overhead signs mean. You are required to obey these signs even if there appear to be no problems ahead. There could be queuing traffic or another hazard that you cannot see yet.

Judge when you are allowed to stop on a motorway. You are required to stop if overhead gantry signs show a red cross above every lane on the motorway. You may move into that lane and continue if it is safe to do so if any of the other lanes does not show a red cross.

You are travelling in the left-hand lane of a three-lane motorway. Judge how you should react to traffic joining from a slip road. Plan well ahead when approaching a slip road. Be prepared to adjust your speed or move to another lane if it is safe to do so if you see traffic joining the motorway. This can help the flow of traffic joining the motorway, especially at peak times.

Judge how you should use the lanes on a motorway. The safe action is to normally travel in the left-hand lane unless you are overtaking a slower-moving vehicle. Move back into the left-hand lane, but do not cut across in front of the vehicle that you have overtaken when you have finished overtaking.

You are travelling along a motorway. Judge when you are allowed to overtake on the left. Never overtake on the left, unless the traffic is moving in queues and the queue on your right is moving more slowly than the one you are in.

Judge when you would use an emergency area on a motorway. On some motorways, emergency areas are built at the side of the carriageway. Try to get your vehicle into the emergency area where there is an emergency telephone if you break down. The phone connects directly to a control centre. You are required to call the control centre - a lane may need to be closed to allow you to rejoin safely before rejoining the motorway.

You are on a motorway. Work out what it means when a red cross is displayed above the hard shoulder. At certain times, the hard shoulder will be open as a running lane. However, a red cross above the hard shoulder shows that it is not open as a running lane and should only be used for emergencies and breakdowns.

You are on a motorway. Work out what it means when a mandatory speed limit is displayed above the hard shoulder. A mandatory speed limit sign above the hard shoulder shows that this part of the road can be used as a running lane between junctions. You are required to stay within the speed limit. Look out for vehicles that may have broken down and could be blocking the hard shoulder.

Understand how bunching is reduced on motorways. You are required to follow the mandatory signs on the gantries above motorway lanes, including the hard shoulder. Variable speed limits help keep the traffic moving and also help to prevent bunching.

Work out what helps to reduce traffic bunching on a motorway. Congestion can be reduced by keeping traffic at a constant speed. At busy times, maximum speed limits are displayed on overhead gantries. These can be varied quickly, depending on the amount of traffic. By keeping to a constant speed on busy sections of motorway, overall journey times are normally improved.

Judge when you may stop on a motorway. Do not normally stop on a motorway, but there may be occasions when it is necessary to do so. Stop on the hard shoulder and use the emergency telephones to call for assistance if your vehicle breaks down or there is an emergency.

You stop on the hard shoulder of a motorway and use the emergency telephone. Judge where the best place to wait for help to arrive. You are at risk of being injured by motorway traffic when you are on the hard shoulder. The safest place to wait is away from the carriageway, but near enough to see the emergency services arriving.

You are on a motorway. Decide what you are required to do if there is a red cross showing above every lane. A red cross signal above all lanes means you are required to stop and wait. Do not change lanes and do not try to continue any further along the motorway.

You are on a motorway. Work out what it means if a red cross is showing above the hard shoulder and mandatory speed limits above all other lanes. A red cross above the hard shoulder shows that it is closed as a running lane and should only be used for emergencies or breakdowns. On some motorways, the hard shoulder may be used as a running lane at busy times. This will be shown by a mandatory speed limit on the gantry above the hard shoulder.

Judge where you should stop to rest if you feel tired while you are travelling along a motorway. Stop at the nearest service area if you feel tired. Leave the motorway at the next exit and find a safe place to stop if that is too far away. Do not stop on the carriageway or hard shoulder of a motorway except in an emergency, when in a traffic queue, or when signalled to do so by a police officer, a traffic officer or traffic signals. Plan your journey so that you have regular rest stops.

Work out the speed limit for a car towing a trailer on a motorway. Light trailer, it will not reduce your vehicle's performance by very much and it may not be visible in your mirrors if you are towing a small. However, strong winds or buffeting from large vehicles might cause the trailer to snake from side to side. Watch for your speed and do not exceed the reduced speed limit imposed on vehicles towing trailers.

Judge when you should use the left-hand lane of a motorway. The safe action is to drive in the left-hand lane whenever possible. Only use the other lanes for overtaking or when directed to do so by signals. Using other lanes when the left-hand lane is empty can frustrate drivers behind you.

You are driving on a motorway and have to slow down suddenly due to a hazard ahead. Judge how you can warn drivers behind of the hazard. Using your hazard warning lights, as well as your brake lights, will give the traffic behind an extra warning of the problem ahead. Only use them for long enough for your warning to be seen.

Your car gets a puncture while you are driving on the motorway. Decide what to do when you have stopped on the hard shoulder. Park as far to the left as you can and leave the vehicle by the nearside door. Do not attempt even simple repairs. Instead, walk to an emergency telephone on your side of the road and phone for help. Stay by your car, keeping well away from the carriageway and hard shoulder while waiting for help to arrive.

Decide what to do if you are driving on a motorway and you miss the exit that you wanted to take. It is illegal to reverse, cross the central reservation or drive against the traffic flow on a motorway. Carry on until you reach the next one if you miss your exit. Ask yourself why you missed your exit – if you think that your concentration is fading, take a break before continuing your journey.

Your vehicle has broken down on a motorway. Decide what to do if you are not able to get onto the hard shoulder. Use your hazard warning lights to warn others if you cannot get your vehicle onto the hard shoulder. Leave your vehicle only when you can safely get clear of the carriageway. Do not try to repair the vehicle or attempt to place any warning device on the carriageway.

Understand why it is particularly important to check your vehicle before making a long motorway journey. Confirm that your vehicle can cope with the demands of high-speed driving before you start your journey. The safe action is to check a number of things; the main ones being fuel, oil, water and tyres. You also need to plan rest stops if you are making a long journey.

You are driving on a motorway. Work out what it means if the car in front shows its hazard warning lights for a short time. There may be an incident, stopped traffic or queuing traffic ahead if the vehicle in front shows its hazard warning lights. By keeping a safe distance from the vehicle in front, you are able to look beyond it and see any hazards well ahead.

You are driving on the motorway. Judge which lane should you get into well before you reach your exit. You will see the first advance direction sign one mile from a motorway exit. You will only have about 50 seconds before you reach the countdown markers if you are travelling at 60 mph in the right-hand lane. There will be another sign at the half-mile point. Do not cut across lanes of traffic at the last moment – move to the left-hand lane in good time.

Your vehicle breaks down on a motorway and you manage to stop on the hard shoulder. Decide what to do if you use your mobile phone to call for help. The safe action is to use an emergency telephone when you break down on the motorway; only use your mobile if this is not possible. The emergency services need to know your exact location so they can reach you as quickly as possible. Look for a number on the nearest marker post beside the hard shoulder. Give this number when you call the emergency services.

You are towing a trailer along a three-lane motorway. Judge when you may use the right-hand lane. Do not use the right-hand lane of a motorway with 3 or more lanes except in certain specified circumstances, such as when lanes are closed if you are towing a caravan or trailer.

Work out what would you expect to find at a contraflow system on a motorway. Reduce speed in good time and obey all speed limits when approaching a contraflow system. You may be travelling in a narrower lane than normal, with no permanent barrier between you and the oncoming traffic. Stay alert that the hard shoulder may be used for traffic and the road ahead could be obstructed by slow-moving or broken-down vehicles.

You are waiting to turn right out of a minor road. It is clear to the left but a lorry is coming from the right. Understand why you should wait, even if you have enough time to turn. Large vehicles can hide other vehicles that are overtaking – especially motorcycles. It is necessary to watch for the possibility of hidden vehicles and not assume that it is safe to turn.

You are following a long vehicle as it approaches a crossroads. Decide what to do if it signals left but moves out to the right. A long vehicle may need to swing out in the opposite direction as it approaches a turn, to allow the rear wheels to clear the kerb. Do not try to filter through if you see a gap; as the lorry turns, the gap will close.

You are following a long vehicle approaching a crossroads. Decide what to do if the driver signals right but moves close to the left-hand kerb.
