It may need to keep close to the left-hand kerb when a long vehicle is going to turn right. This is to prevent the rear end of the trailer cutting the corner. It is necessary to watch for how long vehicles behave in such situations. Do not overtake the lorry, because it could turn as you are alongside. Stay behind and wait for it to turn.

You are approaching a mini-roundabout. Decide what to do if a long vehicle in front signals left but positions over to the right. At mini-roundabouts, there is not much room for a long vehicle to manoeuvre. It will have to swing out wide so that it can complete the turn safely. Keep well back and do not try to move up alongside it.

You are travelling on a single carriageway road. Understand why you should keep well back while you are following a large vehicle. Keep well back when following a large vehicle. You will not be able to see the road ahead and the driver of the long vehicle might not be able to see you in their mirrors if you are too close.

You are travelling behind a bus. Decide what to do if it pulls up at a bus stop. People may be running to catch the bus or passengers leaving the bus might wish to cross the road in front of the bus. Look out for them if you intend to go past it. Consider how many people are waiting to get on the bus – check the queue if you can. The bus might move off straight away if no-one is waiting to get on. Give it priority if it is safe to do so if a bus is signalling to pull out.

You are following a lorry on a wet road. Decide what to do when spray makes it difficult to see the road ahead. Large vehicles can throw up a lot of spray when it is wet. This makes it difficult for drivers behind to see the road ahead. You will be able to see more by dropping back further, out of the spray. This will also increase your separation distance, giving you more room to stop if you have to.

You are leaving a safe gap as you follow a large vehicle. Decide what to do if a car moves into this gap. Sometimes your separation distance is shortened by a driver moving into the gap you have allowed. React positively, stay calm and drop further back to re-establish a safe following distance when this happens.

Decide what to do when you are approaching a bus that is signalling to move away from a bus stop. Try to give way to buses if you can do so safely, especially when the driver signals to pull away from a bus stop. Look out for people getting off the bus or running to catch it, because they may cross the road without looking. Do not accelerate to get past the bus, and do not flash your lights, as this could mislead other road users.

Decide what to do if you want to overtake a long, slow-moving vehicle on a busy road. Stay well back so that you can get a better view of the road ahead when you are following a long vehicle. The closer you get, the less you will be able to see of the road. Be patient and do not take a gamble. Only overtake when you are certain that you can complete the manoeuvre safely.

Judge which vehicles are least likely to be affected by side wind. Although cars are the least likely to be affected, side winds can take anyone by surprise. This is most likely to happen after overtaking a large vehicle, when passing gaps between hedges or buildings, and on exposed sections of road.

Decide what to do as you approach this lorry. Long vehicles need much more room on the road than other vehicles when turning. At junctions, they may take up the whole of the road space, so be patient and allow them the room they need.

You are following a large vehicle as it approaches a crossroads. Decide what to do if the driver signals to turn left. Hold back and wait until the vehicle has turned before proceeding. Do not overtake, because the vehicle turning left could hide another vehicle emerging from the same junction.

Understand why it is more difficult to overtake a large vehicle than a car. Depending on relative speed, it will usually take you longer to pass a lorry than other vehicles. Hazards to watch for include oncoming traffic, junctions ahead, bends or dips that could restrict your view, and signs or road markings that prohibit overtaking. Confirm you can see that it is safe to complete the manoeuvre before you start to overtake.

It is very windy. Decide what to do if you are behind a motorcyclist who is overtaking a high-sided vehicle. Windy weather affects motorcyclists more than other vehicles. In windy conditions, high-sided vehicles cause air turbulence. The safe action is to keep well back, as the motorcyclist could be blown off course.

Decide what to do if there is a bus at a bus stop ahead of you. As you approach, look out for any signal the driver might make. Watch out for pedestrians attempting to cross the road from behind the bus if you pass the vehicle. They will be hidden from view until the last moment.

Work out what should you be prepared to do in this situation. Sometimes, large vehicles may need more space than other road users. Be prepared to stop and wait if a vehicle needs more time and space to turn.

Understand why should drivers be more careful on roads where trams also operate. The safe action is to take extra care when you first encounter trams. You will have to get used to dealing with a different traffic system. Stay alert that trams can accelerate and travel very quickly, and they cannot change direction to avoid obstructions.

You are towing a caravan. Judge which is the safest type of rear-view mirror to use. Towing a large trailer or caravan can greatly reduce your view of the road behind. You may need to fit extended-arm side mirrors so that you can see clearly behind and down both sides of the caravan or trailer.

You are driving in heavy traffic on a wet road. Judge which lights should you use if there is a lot of surface spray. You are required to confirm that other road users can see you, but you do not want to dazzle them. Use your dipped headlights during the day if visibility is poor. You may use your rear fog lights, but do not forget to turn them off when the visibility improves if visibility falls below 100 metres (328 feet).

Decide what to do if you overtake a cyclist when it is very windy. Cyclists, and motorcyclists, are very vulnerable in high winds. They can easily be blown well off course and veer into your path. Always allow plenty of room when overtaking them. Passing too close could cause a draught and unbalance the rider.

Judge when you should use your vehicle's horn. Do not use your vehicle's horn between 11:30pm and 7am in a built-up area or when you are stationary, unless a moving vehicle poses a danger. Its function is to alert other road users to your presence.

You are about to overtake. Decide what to do when you see this sign. You will not be able to see any hazards that might be hidden in the dip. As well as oncoming traffic, the dip may conceal • cyclists • horse riders • parked vehicles • pedestrians in the road.

You are at a junction controlled by traffic lights. Judge when you should wait at a green light. As you approach the traffic lights, look into the road you wish to take. Only proceed if your exit road is clear. Hold back, even if you have to wait for the next green signal if the road is blocked.

Judge who has priority when traffic lights are out of order. The safe action is to treat the junction as an unmarked crossroads when traffic lights are out of order. Be cautious, as you may need to give way or stop. Look for traffic attempting to cross the junction, unaware that it does not have priority.

Judge when you may cross a double solid white line in the middle of the road. You may cross the solid white line to pass a stationary vehicle or to pass a cyclist, horse or road maintenance vehicle if it is travelling at 10 mph or less. You may also cross the solid white line to enter a side road or access a property.

Understand why this junction have a 'stop' sign and a stop line on the road. Where emerging traffic has a very restricted view of the main road, you may find a 'stop' sign and a solid white stop line. You are required to stop at the line and then check carefully before you emerge.

Judge how a police officer in a patrol vehicle signal for you to stop. You are required to obey signals given by the police. They will indicate this without causing danger to you or other traffic if a police officer in a patrol vehicle wants you to pull over.

You are approaching a junction where the traffic lights are not working. Decide what to do when a police officer gives this signal. You are required to obey them when a police officer or traffic warden is directing traffic. They will use the arm signals shown in The Highway Code. Learn what these signals mean and obey them.

Judge how the right-hand lane of a three-lane motorway should be used. The safe action is to stay in the left-hand lane of a motorway unless you are overtaking another vehicle. The right-hand lane of a motorway is an overtaking lane; it is not the 'fast lane'. Move back to the left when it is safe to do so after overtaking.
Judge where you can find reflective amber studs on a motorway. At night or in poor visibility, reflective studs on the road help you to judge your position on the carriageway.

Judge where you would find green reflective studs on a motorway. Knowing the colours of the reflective studs on the road will help you judge your position, especially at night, in foggy conditions or when visibility is poor.

Decide what to do when you see this sign as you travel along a motorway. You will see this sign if the motorway is closed ahead. Pull into the left-hand lane as soon as it is safe to do so. Do not wait until the last moment before you move across, because the lane may be busy and you will have to rely on another driver making room for you.

Decide what to do when you see this sign at a crossroads. Treat the junction as an unmarked crossroads when traffic lights are out of order. Be very careful and be prepared to stop; no-one has priority.

You are on a motorway. A lorry has stopped in the right-hand lane. Decide what to do when you see this sign on the lorry. Sometimes work is carried out on the motorway without closing the lanes. Signs are mounted on the back of lorries to warn other road users of the roadworks ahead when this happens.

You are on a motorway. Decide what to do if there is a red cross showing on the signs above your lane only. A red cross above your lane shows that your lane is closed. The safe action is to move into another lane as soon as you can do so safely.

Judge when you may sound your vehicle's horn. Never sound your vehicle's horn aggressively. Do not sound it in a built-up area between 11:30pm and 7am, or when you are stationary, unless another road user poses a danger. Do not scare animals by sounding your horn.

Your vehicle is stationary. Judge when you may use its horn. Only sound the horn if you think there is a risk of danger from another road user when your vehicle is stationary. Do not use it just to attract someone's attention. This causes unnecessary noise and could be misleading.

A police car is following you. Decide what to do if the police officer flashes the headlights and points to the left. You are required to pull up on the left as soon as it is safe to do so and switch off your engine.

Work out what it means if you see this signal on the motorway. You will see this sign if there has been an incident ahead and the motorway is closed. You are required to obey the sign. Confirm that you prepare to leave in good time. Do not cause drivers to take avoiding action by cutting in at the last moment.

Decide what you are required to do when you see this sign. 'Stop' signs are situated at junctions where visibility is restricted or where there is heavy traffic. They must be obeyed: you are required to stop. Look carefully before moving off.

Decide what to do when you are approaching traffic lights that have red and amber showing together. Stay alert that other traffic might still be clearing the junction as you approach. A green light means you may go on, but only if the way is clear.

You have stopped at a railway level crossing. Decide what to do if the red lights continue to flash after a train has gone by. Always obey red flashing stop lights. Another train will be passing soon if a train passes but the lights continue to flash. Cross only when the lights go off and the barriers open.

Work out what should you be aware of if you have just passed this sign. In a one-way system, traffic may pass you on either side. Always watch for all traffic signs and understand their meaning. Look well ahead and react to them in good time.

You are approaching traffic lights and the red light is showing. Work out what signal will show next. You can plan your approach accordingly if you know which light is going to show next. This can help prevent excessive braking or hesitation at the junction.

Judge how you should give an arm signal to turn left. There may be occasions when other road users are unable to see your indicator, such as in bright sunlight or at a busy, complicated junction. In these cases, an arm signal will help others to understand your intentions.

You are waiting at a T-junction. Decide what to do if a vehicle is coming from the right, with its left indicator flashing. Other road users may give misleading signals. Do not emerge until you are sure of their intentions when you are waiting at a junction.

Judge when you may use hazard warning lights while you are driving. Briefly showing your hazard warning lights will help alert the traffic behind to the hazard when there is queuing traffic ahead and you have to slow down or even stop.

Understand why you should make sure that your indicators are cancelled after turning at a junction. Leaving your indicators on could confuse other road users and may even lead to a crash. Stay alert that if you have not turned sharply, your indicators may not self-cancel and you will need to turn them off manually.

You are driving in busy traffic. You want to pull up just after a junction on the left. Judge when you should signal. It is necessary to signal to let other drivers know your intentions. However, if you indicate too early, they may think you are turning left into the junction. Correct timing of the signal is very important to avoid misleading others.

There are no speed limit signs on the road. Keep this situation in mind: in England, Scotland and Northern Ireland how is a 30 mph limit generally indicated. In England, Scotland and Northern Ireland, there is a 30 mph speed limit where there are street lights, unless signs show another limit. In Wales, street lights indicate the limit is 20 mph, unless signs show otherwise.

In England, Scotland and Northern Ireland. Work out what the speed limit will usually be where you can see street lights but no speed limit signs. In England, Scotland and Northern Ireland, the presence of street lights generally indicates that there is a 30 mph speed limit, unless signs tell you otherwise. In Wales, street lights indicate a 20 mph limit, unless signs show otherwise.

Decide what to do if you want to overtake a tractor but are not sure that it is safe. Following a tractor can be frustrating, but never overtake if you are unsure whether it is safe. Ask yourself: 'Can I see far enough down the road to be sure that I can complete the manoeuvre safely?' it is better to be delayed for a minute or 2 than to take a chance that may cause a collision.

Judge which vehicle is most likely to take an unusual course at a roundabout. Long vehicles might have to take a slightly different position when approaching the roundabout or going around it. This is to stop the rear of the vehicle cutting in and mounting the kerb.

Judge when you may stop on a clearway. Clearways are in place so that traffic can flow without the obstruction of parked vehicles. Just one parked vehicle can cause an obstruction for all other traffic. Do not stop where a clearway is in force, not even to pick up or set down passengers.

You are looking for somewhere to park at night. Judge when you may park on the right-hand side of the road. Red rear reflectors show up when headlights shine on them. These are useful when you are parked at night, but they will only reflect if you park in the same direction as the traffic flow. Normally the safe action is to park on the left, but in a one-way street you may also park on the right-hand side of the road.

Judge when you should use the right-hand lane of a three-lane dual carriageway. The safe action is to normally use the left-hand lane on any dual carriageway unless you are overtaking or turning right. Look for vehicles ahead that are turning right when overtaking on a dual carriageway. They may be slowing or stopped. It is necessary to see them in good time so that you can take appropriate action.

You are approaching a busy junction. Decide what to do when, at the last moment, you realise you are in the wrong lane. There are times when road markings are obscured by queuing traffic, or you are unsure which lane to use. If, at the last moment, you find you are in the wrong lane, do not cut across or bully other drivers to let you in. Follow the lane you are in and find somewhere safe to turn around and rejoin your route.

Judge where you may overtake on a one-way street. You can overtake other traffic on either side when travelling in a one-way street. Make full use of your mirrors and confirm it is clear all around before you attempt to overtake. Look for signs and road markings, and use the most suitable lane for your destination.

Work out what signal should you give when you are going straight ahead at a roundabout. Do not signal as you approach it when going straight ahead at a roundabout. Signal left just after passing the exit before the one you wish to take.

Judge which vehicle might have to take a different course from normal at a roundabout. A long vehicle may have to straddle lanes either on or approaching a roundabout so that the rear wheels do not mount the kerb. Stay well back and give it plenty of room if you are following a long vehicle.

Judge when you may enter a box junction. Yellow box junctions are marked on the road to prevent the road becoming blocked. Do not enter the box unless your exit road is clear. You may wait in the box if you want to turn right and your exit road is clear but oncoming traffic or other vehicles waiting to turn right are preventing you from making the turn.

Judge when you may stop and wait in a box junction. The purpose of yellow box markings is to keep junctions clear of queuing traffic. You may only wait in the marked area when you are turning right and your exit lane is clear but you cannot complete the turn because of oncoming traffic or other traffic waiting to turn right.

Judge who is authorised to signal you to stop. You are required to obey signals to stop given by police and traffic officers, traffic wardens and school crossing patrols. Failure to do so is an offence and could lead to prosecution.

Decide what to do if you see a pedestrian waiting at a zebra crossing. By standing on the pavement, the pedestrian is showing an intention to cross. By looking well ahead, you will give yourself time to see the pedestrian, check your mirrors and respond safely.

Judge which road users benefit from toucan crossings. Toucan crossings are similar to pelican crossings but there is no flashing amber phase. Cyclists share the crossing with pedestrians and are allowed to cycle across when the green bicycle symbol is shown.

You are waiting at a pelican crossing. Work out what it means when the red light changes to flashing amber. This light allows pedestrians already on the crossing to get to the other side in their own time, without being rushed. Do not rev your engine or start to move off while they are still crossing.

You see these double white lines along the centre of the road. Judge when you may park on the left. Do not park or stop on a road marked with double white lines (even where one of the lines is broken) except to pick up or set down passengers.

You are turning right at a crossroads. An oncoming driver is also turning right. Work out the advantage of turning behind the oncoming vehicle. It is generally safer to turn behind the approaching vehicle when turning right at a crossroads where oncoming traffic is also turning right. This allows you a clear view of approaching traffic and is called 'turning offside to offside'. However, some junctions, usually controlled by traffic-light filters - are marked for vehicles to turn nearside to nearside.

You are travelling along a residential street. There are parked vehicles on the left-hand side. Understand why you should keep your speed down. Travel slowly and carefully near parked vehicles. Beware of • vehicles pulling out, especially bicycles and motorcycles • pedestrians, especially children, who may run out from between cars • drivers opening their doors.

Decide what to do when there is an obstruction on your side of the road. Take care if you have to pass an obstruction, such as a parked vehicle, on your side of the road. Give way to oncoming traffic if there is not enough room for you both to continue safely.

Judge when you would use the right-hand lane of a two-lane dual carriageway. Normally the safe action is to travel in the left-hand lane and only use the right-hand lane for overtaking or turning right. Move back into the left lane as soon as it is safe but do not cut in across the path of the vehicle you have just passed.
Judge who has priority at an unmarked crossroads. Practise good observation in all directions before you emerge or make a turn. Proceed only when you are sure it is safe to do so.

Work out the nearest you may park to a junction. Do not park within 10 metres (32 feet) of a junction (unless in an authorised parking place). This is to allow drivers emerging from, or turning into, the junction a clear view of the road they are joining. It also allows them to see hazards such as pedestrians or cyclists at the junction.

You are looking for somewhere to safely park your vehicle. Judge where you would choose to park. It may be tempting to park where do not while you run a quick errand. Careless parking is a selfish act and could endanger other road users.

You are waiting at a level crossing. Decide what you are required to do if a train passes but the lights keep flashing. The safe action is to continue to wait, because another train might be coming if the lights at a level crossing keep flashing after a train has passed. Time seems to pass slowly when you are held up in a queue. Be patient and wait until the lights stop flashing.

Decide what you are required to do if you come across roadworks that have a temporary speed limit displayed. Where there are extra hazards, such as at roadworks, it is often necessary to slow traffic by imposing a lower speed limit. These speed limits are not advisory; they must be obeyed.

You are in a built-up area at night and the road is well lit. Understand why you should use dipped headlights. You may be difficult to see when you are travelling at night, even on a well-lit road. Other road users should be able to see you more easily if you use dipped headlights rather than sidelights.

You are turning right onto a dual carriageway. Decide what to do if the central reservation is too narrow to contain your vehicle. It may not be able to contain your vehicle when the central reservation is narrow. In this case, the safe action is to treat a dual carriageway as one road. Wait until the road is clear in both directions before emerging to turn right. Your vehicle will stick out and cause an obstruction that may lead to a collision if you try to treat it as 2 separate roads and wait in the middle.

Decide what to do when you park at night on a road that has a 40 mph speed limit. You are required to use parking lights when parking at night on a road or in a lay-by on a road with a speed limit greater than 30 mph. You are required to also park in the direction of the traffic flow and not close to a junction.

You are travelling on a motorway in England. Judge when you are required to stop your vehicle. You will find traffic officers on motorways and some primary routes in England and Wales. They work in partnership with the police, helping to keep traffic moving and helping to make your journey as safe as possible. It is an offence not to comply with the directions given by a traffic officer.

Judge how you should signal if you are going straight ahead at a roundabout. To go straight ahead at a roundabout, the safe action is to normally approach in the left-hand lane, but check the road markings. At some roundabouts, the left lane on approach is marked 'left turn only', so confirm you use the correct lane to go ahead. You will not normally need to signal as you approach, but signal before you leave the roundabout, as other road users need to know your intentions.
Judge when you may drive over a pavement. It is illegal to drive on or over a pavement, except to gain access to a property. Give priority to pedestrians if it is necessary to cross a pavement.

Work out the speed limit for a car towing a caravan on a dual carriageway. The speed limit for cars towing caravans or trailers on dual carriageways or motorways is 60 mph. Due to the increased weight and size of the combination, the safe action is to plan further ahead. Take care in windy weather, as a strong side wind can make a caravan or large trailer unstable.

You want to park and you see this sign. Decide what to do on the days and times shown. Parking restrictions apply in a variety of places and situations. Confirm you know the rules and understand where and when restrictions apply. Controlled parking areas will be indicated by signs and road markings. Parking in the wrong place could cause an obstruction and danger to other traffic. It can also result in a fine.

You are going to turn left from a main road into a minor road. Decide what to do as you approach the junction. Your road position can help other road users to anticipate your actions. Keep to the left as you approach a left turn and do not swing out into the centre of the road so you can make the turn easier. This could endanger oncoming traffic and may cause other road users to misunderstand your intentions.

You are waiting at a level crossing. Decide what to do if the red warning lights continue to flash after a train has passed by. At a level crossing, flashing red lights mean you are required to stop. Wait if the train passes but the lights keep flashing. Another train may be coming.

Decide what to do if the amber lights come on and a warning sounds while you are driving over a level crossing. Keep going; do not stop on the crossing. You are required to stop unless it is unsafe to do so if the warning sounds and the amber lights come on as you are approaching the crossing. Red flashing lights together with the audible warning mean you are required to stop.

You are driving on a busy main road. Decide what to do if you find that you are driving in the wrong direction. Do not turn around in a busy street or reverse from a side road into a main road. Find a quiet side road and choose a place to turn around where you will not obstruct an entrance or exit. Look out for pedestrians and cyclists as well as other traffic.

Judge when you may drive without wearing your seat belt. You may remove your seat belt while you are carrying out a manoeuvre that includes reversing. However, you are required to remember to put it back on again before you resume driving.

Judge how far you are allowed to reverse. Do not reverse further than is necessary. You may decide to turn your vehicle around by reversing into an opening or side road. Always look all around you and watch for pedestrians when you reverse. Do not reverse from a side road into a main road.

Decide what to do when you are unsure whether it is safe to reverse your vehicle. A small child could be hidden directly behind you, so, if you cannot see all around your vehicle, get out and have a look. You could also ask someone reliable outside the vehicle to guide you.

Understand why could it be dangerous to reverse from a side road into a main road. Do not reverse into a main road from a side road because your view will be restricted. The main road is likely to be busy and the traffic on it moving quickly.

You want to turn right at a box junction. Decide what to do if there is oncoming traffic. You can wait in the box junction as long as your exit is clear. At some point there will be a gap in the oncoming traffic, or the traffic lights will change, allowing you to proceed.

You are reversing into a side road. Keep this situation in mind: when would your vehicle be the greatest hazard to passing traffic. Always check in all directions before reversing. Keep a good lookout throughout the manoeuvre and remember that the front will swing out as you reverse into the side road. Act on what you see and wait if necessary.

Judge where the safest place to park your vehicle at night. Use it if you have a garage. Your vehicle is less likely to be a victim of car crime if it is in a garage. Also, in winter, the windows will be kept free from ice and snow.
Judge when you may stop on an urban clearway. Urban clearways have their times of operation clearly signed. You may only stop to pick up or set down passengers.

You are looking for somewhere to park your vehicle. Neither you or your passenger are disabled. Decide what to do if the only free spaces are marked for disabled drivers. It is illegal to park in a space reserved for disabled drivers unless you are permitted to do so. These spaces are provided for people with limited mobility, who may need extra space to get in and out of their vehicle.

You are on a road that is only wide enough for one vehicle. Decide what to do if a car is coming towards you. Pull into the nearest passing place on the left if you meet another vehicle on a narrow road. Wait opposite it if the nearest passing place is on the right.

You are driving at night with your headlights on main beam. A vehicle is overtaking you. Judge when you should dip your headlights. On main beam, your lights could dazzle the driver in front. Dip your headlights as soon as the driver passes you and drop back so that the dipped beam falls short of the vehicle in front.

Judge when you may drive a car in this bus lane. Some bus lanes operate only during peak hours and other vehicles may use them outside these hours. Confirm you check the sign for the hours of operation before driving in a bus lane.

Other than direction indicators. Judge how you can give signals to other road users. Your brake lights will give an indication to traffic behind that you are slowing down. Good anticipation will allow you time to check your mirrors before slowing.

You are parked in a busy high street. Work out the safest way to turn your vehicle around so you can drive in the opposite direction. Confirm you carry out the manoeuvre without causing a hazard to other vehicles. Choose a place to turn that is safe and considers other road users.
Judge where you should park your vehicle at night. Park in a well-lit area when you are parking at night. This can help deter criminals from targeting your vehicle.

You are driving in the right-hand lane of a dual carriageway. Decide what to do if you see a sign showing that the right-hand lane is closed 800 yards ahead. Keep a lookout for traffic signs. Do so in good time if you are directed to change lanes. Do not • push your way into traffic in another lane • try to gain advantage by delaying changing lanes.

Judge when you are allowed to park in a parking bay for disabled drivers. Do not park in a space reserved for disabled people unless you or your passenger are a Blue Badge holder. The badge must be displayed on the dashboard or fascia panel, where it can be clearly read through the front windscreen.

Judge when you are required to stop your vehicle. You are required to stop your vehicle when signalled to do so by a • police, DVSA or traffic officer • traffic warden • school crossing patrol • red traffic light. You are required to also stop if you are involved in an incident that causes damage or injury to any other person, vehicle, animal or property.

Decide what to do if your anti-lock braking system (ABS) warning light stays on. Consult the vehicle handbook or a garage before driving the vehicle any further. Only drive to a garage if it is safe to do so. Get expert help if you are not sure.

Understand why it is important to wear suitable shoes when you are driving. Confirm that you are wearing suitable clothing when you are going to drive. Comfortable shoes will allow you to keep proper control of the foot pedals.

Judge how a roof rack affect your car. A roof rack increases your car's wind resistance. This will cause an increase in fuel consumption, so the safe action is to remove it when it is not being used. An aerodynamically designed roof rack or box will help reduce wind resistance to a minimum, but the rack or box should still be removed when it is not in use.

Judge how you can avoid wasting fuel. The engine will gradually become less efficient if you do not have your vehicle serviced regularly. This will cause increased fuel consumption and, in turn, an increase in the amount of harmful emissions it produces.

Decide what you could do to reduce the volume of traffic on the roads. Try not to use your car unnecessarily. For shorter journeys, consider walking or cycling instead - this is much better for both you and the environment.

Decide what to do if your vehicle pulls to one side when you use the brakes. The brakes on your vehicle must be effective and properly adjusted. Take it to be checked by a qualified mechanic as soon as you can if your vehicle pulls to one side when braking.

Work out what will happen if your car's wheels are unbalanced. It will cause the steering to vibrate at certain speeds if your wheels are out of balance. This is not a fault that will put itself right, so take your vehicle to a garage or tyre fitter to have the wheels rebalanced.

Work out what should you remove from your car before leaving it unattended. Never leave the vehicle registration document inside your car. This document would help a thief to dispose of your car more easily.

Decide what to do when leaving your vehicle parked and unattended. An unlocked car is an open invitation to thieves. Leaving the keys in the ignition not only makes your car easy to steal but could also invalidate your insurance.

You service your own vehicle. Judge how you should dispose of the old engine oil. It is illegal to pour engine oil down any drain. Oil is a pollutant and harmful to wildlife. Dispose of it safely at an authorised site.

Understand why do MOT tests include an exhaust emission test. Emission tests are carried out to confirm your vehicle's engine is operating efficiently. This keeps the pollution produced by the engine to a minimum. It may fail the MOT emissions test if your vehicle is not serviced regularly.

Judge how you can reduce the damage your vehicle causes to the environment. By looking well ahead and recognising hazards in good time, you can avoid late and heavy braking. Watch the traffic flow and look well ahead for potential hazards so you can control your speed in good time. Avoid over-revving the engine and accelerating harshly, as this increases wear to the engine and uses more fuel.

Judge how you benefit from following the manufacturer's service schedule for your vehicle. All vehicles need to be serviced to keep working efficiently. An efficient engine uses less fuel and produces fewer harmful emissions than an engine that is running inefficiently. Keeping the vehicle serviced to the manufacturer's schedule should also keep it reliable and reduce the chance of it breaking down.

Judge how you should drive when you are driving along a road that has road humps. Road humps are there for a reason – to protect vulnerable road users by reducing the speed of traffic. Do not accelerate harshly between the humps. Put the safety of others first and maintain a reduced speed throughout the zone.

Judge when you should check the engine oil level. An engine can use more oil during long journeys than on shorter trips. Insufficient engine oil is potentially dangerous: it can lead to excessive wear, mechanical breakdown and expensive repairs. Most cars have a dipstick to allow the oil level to be checked. The safe action is to refer to the vehicle handbook if not.
Decide what to do when you leave your car unattended for a few minutes. Always switch off the engine, remove the key and lock your car, even if you are only leaving it for a few minutes.
Understand why you should try and park in a secure car park. Whenever possible, leave your car in a secure car park. This will help deter thieves.
Judge how you can reduce the chances of your car being broken into when leaving it unattended. Take all valuables with you if you can when leaving your car. Otherwise, lock them out of sight.
Judge how you can help to prevent your car radio being stolen. A security-coded radio can deter thieves, as it is likely to be of little use when removed from the vehicle.

Judge how you can reduce the risk of your vehicle being broken into at night. Having your vehicle broken into or stolen can be very distressing and inconvenient. Avoid leaving your vehicle unattended in poorly lit areas.

You have to make an unexpected journey. You are carrying a 5-year-old child on the back seat of your car. They are under 1.35 metres (4 feet 5 inches) tall. Judge how you should seat them if a correct child restraint is not available. In journeys of unexpected necessity, and when a correct child restraint is not available, the child must sit on the rear seat and use an adult seat belt. In a collision, unrestrained objects and people can cause serious injury or even death.

You are stopped at the side of the road. Decide what you are required to do if you will be waiting there for some time. You are required to switch off the engine unless you are stationary in traffic or diagnosing a fault if your vehicle is stationary and is likely to remain so for some time.

You want to put a rear-facing baby seat on the front passenger seat. Decide what you are required to do if the passenger seat is protected by a frontal airbag. It is illegal to fit a rear-facing baby seat into a passenger seat protected by an active frontal airbag. It could cause serious injury or even death to the child if the airbag activates. You are required to secure it in a different seat or deactivate the relevant airbag. Follow the manufacturer's advice when fitting a baby seat.

You are leaving your vehicle parked on a road and unattended. Judge when you may leave the engine running. Switch off the engine and secure the vehicle when you leave your vehicle parked on a road. Confirm no valuables are visible, shut all the windows, lock the vehicle, and set the alarm if the vehicle has one.

Understand why have 'red routes' been introduced in major cities. Inconsiderate parking can obstruct the flow of traffic and so make traffic congestion worse. Red routes are designed to prevent this by enforcing strict parking restrictions. Driving slowly in traffic increases fuel consumption and causes a build-up of exhaust fumes.
Judge how you should dispose of a used vehicle battery. Batteries contain acid, which is hazardous, and they must be disposed of safely. This means taking them to an appropriate disposal site.

You are parked on the road at night. Judge when you are required to use parking lights. Park in the direction of the traffic when parking at night. This will allow other road users to see the reflectors on the rear of your vehicle. Use your parking lights if the speed limit is over 30 mph.

Judge how you can reduce the environmental harm caused by your motor vehicle. Engines that burn fossil fuels produce exhaust emissions that are harmful to health. The harder you make the engine work, the more emissions it will produce. Engines also use more fuel and produce higher levels of emissions when they are cold. Anything you can do to reduce your use of fossil fuels will help the environment.

Judge how you can plan your route before starting a long journey. Various route planners are available on the internet. Most of them give you several options, allowing you to choose between the most direct route and quieter roads. They may also identify rest and fuel stops. Print off the directions and take them with you.
Understand why it is a good idea to plan your journey to avoid busy times. No-one likes to spend time in traffic queues. Try to avoid busy times related to school or work travel.

Judge how your journey be affected by travelling outside the busy times of day. Avoid the early morning, late afternoon and early evening 'rush hour' if possible. Doing this should allow you to have a better journey, with fewer delays. This should help you to arrive at your destination feeling less stressed.

You plan your route before starting a journey. Understand why you should also plan an alternative route. It can be frustrating and worrying to find your planned route is blocked by roadworks or diversions. You will feel less stressed and more able to concentrate fully on your driving or riding if you have planned an alternative. It is a good idea to plan an alternative using non-motorway roads if your original route is mostly on motorways. Always carry a map with you just in case it is necessary to refer to it.

You have to arrive on time for an appointment. Judge how you should plan for the journey. Always allow plenty of time for your journey in case of unforeseen problems. Anything can happen; for instance, punctures, breakdowns, road closures, diversions and delays. You will feel less stressed and less inclined to take risks if you are not 'pushed for time'.

You are driving along a motorway and switch on adaptive cruise control. Work out what are you now allowed to do. When using advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) you are responsible for your vehicle and it is necessary to stay in control of the systems. ADAS are not the same as self-driving functions so you are required to remain alert and be ready to intervene if the system does not work correctly.

You are driving a car with blind-spot monitoring function. Work out what you are required to regularly check to make sure that the function will work properly. Blind-spot monitoring works using a system of sensors that alert you to objects in your blind-spots. The function only works correctly if you keep the sensors clean.

You are driving along a quiet motorway. Judge which advanced driver assistance system (ADAS) is most likely to help you. Lane-departure warning alerts you that you are about to leave your lane. This can help you to keep your car positioned safely and prevent a collision if you are drifting towards the lane markings.

Judge how much stopping distances increase in icy conditions. Tyre grip is greatly reduced in icy conditions. For this reason, it is necessary to allow up to 10 times the stopping distance you would allow on dry roads.

Work out what requires extra care when you are driving or riding in windy conditions. Always give cyclists plenty of room when overtaking them. It is necessary to give them even more room when it is windy. A sudden gust could easily blow them off course and into your path.

Understand why you should keep well to the left as you approach a right-hand bend. Keeping to the left as you approach right-hand bends will give you an earlier view around the bend and allow you to see any hazards sooner. It also reduces the risk of collision with any oncoming vehicle that may have drifted over the centre line while taking the bend.

You have just gone through flood water. Decide what to do to make sure your brakes are working properly. Water on the brakes will act as a lubricant, causing them to work less efficiently. Using the brakes lightly as you go along will quickly dry them out.

Work out what will be affected if the road surface becomes soft in very hot weather. It can soften if the road surface becomes very hot. Tyres are unable to grip a soft surface as well as they can a firm dry one. Take care when cornering and braking.

Judge where your vehicle is most likely to be affected by side winds. In windy conditions, care must be taken on exposed roads. A strong gust of wind can blow you off course. Watch out for other road users who are particularly likely to be affected, such as cyclists, motorcyclists, high-sided lorries and vehicles towing trailers.

You are following a vehicle on a wet road. You stay a safe distance behind it. Decide what to do if a driver overtakes you and pulls into the gap you have left. Wet weather will affect the time it takes for you to stop and can affect your control. Your speed should allow you to stop safely and in good time. Ease back until you have regained your stopping distance if another vehicle pulls into the gap you have allowed.

You are travelling on the motorway. Judge how you can lower the risk of a collision when the vehicle behind is following too closely. On busy roads, traffic may still travel at high speeds. Do not follow the vehicle in front too closely. Gradually increase your distance from the vehicle in front by slowing down gently if a driver behind seems to be 'pushing' you. This will give you more space in front if you have to brake, and will reduce the risk of a collision involving several vehicles.

You are following other vehicles in fog. You have your headlights on dipped beam. Work out what else can you do to reduce the chances of being in a collision. Use your headlights on dipped beam when it is foggy. This will help you see and be seen by other road users. Consider using front and rear fog lights if you have them if visibility is seriously reduced. Keep to a sensible speed and do not follow the vehicle in front too closely. You will need to allow twice the normal stopping distance if the road is wet and slippery.

Decide what to do when you are using a contraflow system. In a contraflow system, you will be travelling close to oncoming traffic and sometimes in narrow lanes. The safe action is to get into the correct lane in good time, obey any temporary speed limit signs and keep a safe separation distance from the vehicle ahead.

Judge how you can avoid wheelspin when you are driving on an icy road. Extra caution will be required to avoid loss of control if you are travelling on an icy road. Keeping your speed down and using the highest gear possible will reduce the risk of the tyres losing their grip on this slippery surface.
Work out the main cause of skidding. Skidding is usually caused by driver error. Always adjust your driving to take account of the road and weather conditions.

You are driving in freezing conditions. Decide what to do as you approach a sharp bend. Harsh use of the accelerator, brakes or steering is likely to lead to skidding, especially on slippery surfaces. Avoid steering and braking at the same time. In icy conditions, it is very important that you constantly assess what is ahead so that you can take appropriate action in plenty of time.

You are about to start a journey in freezing weather. Work out what part of your vehicle should you clear of ice and snow. Driving in bad weather increases your risk of having a collision. Clear your lights, mirrors, number plates and windows of any snow or ice, so that you can see and be seen if you absolutely have to travel.

Work out what will help you to move off on a snowy surface. There will be more torque (turning force) at the driven wheels than if you use a higher gear if you attempt to move off in a low gear. More torque makes it easier for the tyres to lose grip and so spin the wheels.

Decide what to do when you are driving in snowy conditions. In snowy conditions, be careful with the steering, accelerator and brakes. Braking sharply while you are driving on snow is likely to make your car skid.

Work out the main benefit of driving a four-wheel-drive vehicle. By driving all 4 wheels, the vehicle has maximum grip on the road. This grip is especially helpful when travelling on slippery or uneven surfaces. However, having four-wheel drive does not replace the skills it is necessary to drive safely.

You are about to go down a steep hill. Decide what to do to control the speed of your vehicle. Gravity will cause your vehicle to speed up when driving down a steep hill. This will make it more difficult for you to stop. To help keep your vehicle's speed under control, select a lower gear to give you more engine braking and make careful use of the brakes.

Decide what to do when you park a car facing downhill. Turning the wheels towards the kerb will allow them to act as a chock, preventing any forward movement of the vehicle. It will also help to leave your car in gear, or select 'Park' if you have an automatic.

You are driving in a built-up area that has traffic-calming measures. Decide what to do when you approach a road hump. Many towns have road humps as part of traffic-calming measures, designed to slow down traffic. Reduce your speed when driving over them. You could lose control or damage your car if you go too fast. Look out for pedestrians or cyclists while you are driving in these areas.

Judge the road surface where anti-lock brakes may be ineffective. Poor contact with the road surface could cause one or more of the tyres to lose grip on the road. This is more likely to happen when braking in poor weather conditions and when the road has a loose, slippery or uneven surface.

You are driving a vehicle that has an anti-lock braking system (ABS). Judge how you should apply the footbrake when you need to stop in an emergency. You may have to stop in an emergency due to a misjudgement by another driver or a hazard arising suddenly, such as a child running out into the road. The safe action is to apply the brakes immediately and keep them firmly applied until you stop if your vehicle has ABS.

You are driving along a country road. You see this sign. Decide what to do after dealing safely with the hazard. The safe action is to check that they are working properly before you build up speed again if your brakes have been thoroughly soaked. Remember to check your mirrors and consider what is behind you before you do this.

Work out what would suggest you are driving on an icy road. Drive extremely carefully when the roads are icy. Tyres make virtually no noise and the steering feels light and unresponsive when travelling on ice. In icy conditions, be very gentle when braking, accelerating and steering.

You are driving along a wet road. Judge how you can tell if your vehicle's tyres are losing their grip on the surface. Your steering may suddenly feel lighter than usual if you drive at speed in very wet conditions. This means that the tyres have lifted off the surface of the road and are floating on the surface of the water. This is known as aquaplaning. Reduce speed but do not brake until your steering returns to normal.
Judge in which conditions your overall stopping distance will increase. Extra care should be taken in wet weather. On wet roads, your stopping distance could be double that in dry conditions.

You are driving on an open road in dry weather. Work out what distance should you keep from the vehicle in front. One way of checking there is a safe distance between you and the vehicle in front is to use the two-second rule. To check for a two-second time gap, choose a stationary object ahead, such as a bridge or road sign. Say 'Only a fool breaks the two-second rule' when the car in front passes the object. You are too close and need to increase the gap if you reach the object before you finish saying the phrase.

Judge how you can use your vehicle's engine as a brake. Selecting a lower gear gives increased engine braking when driving on downhill stretches of road. This will prevent excessive use of the brakes, which become less effective if they overheat.

Judge how you should use anti-lock brakes when you need to stop in an emergency. Keep your foot firmly on the brake pedal until the vehicle has stopped if you have an anti-lock braking system (ABS) and need to stop in an emergency. You may hear a grating sound and feel vibration through the brake pedal when the ABS operates. This is normal and the safe action is to maintain pressure on the brake pedal until the vehicle stops.

Work out what lights should you use when you are driving on a wet motorway and vehicles are throwing up surface spray. Switch on your headlights on dipped beam when surface spray reduces visibility. This will help other road users to see you.

Work out what can result when you travel for long distances in neutral (known as coasting). Coasting is the term used when the clutch is held down, or the gear lever is in neutral, and the vehicle is allowed to freewheel. This reduces the driver's control of the vehicle. The engine cannot drive the wheels to stabilise you through a corner, or give the assistance of engine braking to help slow the car when you coast.

Decide what to do before starting a journey in foggy weather. Do not venture out if your journey is not necessary. Let them know that you will be taking longer than usual for your journey if you have to travel and someone is expecting you at the other end. This will stop them worrying if you do not turn up on time and will also take the pressure off you, so you do not feel you have to rush.

Decide what to do when you are overtaking a motorcyclist on a windy day. In strong winds, riders of two-wheeled vehicles are particularly vulnerable. Allow plenty of room when you overtake them. Check to the left as you pass to confirm they are safe.

Work out what it means if the Electronic Stability Control (ESC) indicator light comes on briefly while you are driving. ESC is a computer controlled technology that detects reduced traction and automatically makes corrective adjustments to prevent loss of control. The ESC light comes on briefly to alert the driver that the system has activated and the car is approaching its handling limits. It is a powerful driver aid but it cannot save a car once its traction limits have been exceeded.

Work out what will happen to your car when you drive up a steep hill. The engine will need more power to pull the vehicle up the hill. When approaching a steep hill the safe action is to select a lower gear to help maintain your speed. The safe action is to do this without hesitation, so that you do not lose too much speed before engaging the lower gear.

You are driving on the motorway in windy conditions. Decide what to do as you overtake a high-sided vehicle. The draught caused by other vehicles – particularly those with high sides – could be strong enough to push you out of your lane. Be prepared for a sudden gust of wind as you overtake large vehicles. Keep both hands on the steering wheel to help you keep full control.

You are driving in fog. Understand why you should keep well back from the vehicle in front. Stay well back if you are following another road user in fog. The driver in front will not be able to see hazards until they are close and might need to brake suddenly. Also, the road surface is likely to be wet and could be slippery.

Decide what to do if you park on the road when it is foggy. Try to find a place to park off the road if you have to park your vehicle in foggy conditions. Park on the road facing in the same direction as the traffic if this is not possible. Leave your parking lights switched on and confirm they are clean.

You are driving at night. Decide what to do if you are dazzled by headlights coming towards you. Slow down or, if necessary, stop if the headlights of an oncoming vehicle dazzle you. Do not close your eyes or swerve, as you will increase your chances of having a collision. Do not flash your headlights either, as this could dazzle other drivers and make the situation worse.

Judge when front fog lights may be used. Your fog lights must only be used when visibility is reduced to 100 metres (328 feet) or less. It is necessary to be familiar with the layout of your dashboard so you are aware if your fog lights have been switched on in error, or you have forgotten to switch them off.

You are driving with your front fog lights switched on. Decide what to do if the fog has cleared. Switch off your fog lights if the weather improves, but be prepared to use them again if visibility reduces to less than 100 metres (328 feet).

Understand why you should switch off your rear fog lights when the fog has cleared. Do not forget to switch off your fog lights when the weather improves. You could be prosecuted for driving with them on in good visibility. The high intensity of rear fog lights can dazzle drivers behind and make your brake lights difficult to notice.

Work out what will happen if you use rear fog lights in good conditions. Rear fog lights shine more brightly than normal rear lights, so that they show up in reduced visibility. You are required to switch them off; this stops them dazzling the driver behind when the visibility improves.

Understand why would you fit chains to your wheels. Chains can be fitted to your wheels in snowy conditions. They can help you to move off without wheelspin, or to keep moving in deep snow. You will still need to adjust your driving to suit these conditions.

Judge how you can use your vehicle's engine to control your speed. The safe action is to brake and slow down before selecting a lower gear. The gear can then be used to keep the speed low and help you control the vehicle. This is particularly helpful on long downhill stretches, where brake fade can occur if the brakes overheat.

Understand why could it be dangerous to keep the clutch down, or select neutral, for long periods of time while you are driving. Letting your vehicle roll or coast in neutral reduces your control over steering and braking. This can be dangerous on downhill slopes, where your vehicle could pick up speed very quickly.

You are driving on an icy road. Work out what distance from the car in front should you drive. Do not travel in icy or snowy weather unless your journey is essential. Drive extremely carefully when roads are or may be icy. Stopping distances can be ten times greater than on dry roads.

Judge which lights must you use if you are driving on a well-lit motorway at night. Always use your headlights, even if the road is well lit if you are driving on a motorway at night or in poor visibility. Other road users must be able to see you, but the safe action is to avoid causing dazzle.

You are driving on a motorway at night. Judge which lights should you have on if there are other vehicles just ahead of you. Use dipped headlights if you are driving behind other traffic on the motorway at night. Main-beam headlights will dazzle the other drivers. Your headlights' dipped beam should fall short of the vehicle in front.

Work out what will affect your vehicle's stopping distance. Having tyres correctly inflated and in good condition will confirm they have maximum grip on the road; how well your tyres grip the road has a significant effect on your car's stopping distance.
Judge when you will feel the effects of engine braking. You will feel the effect of engine braking when you take your foot off the accelerator. Changing to a lower gear will increase the effect.

Judge which lights should you switch on when daytime visibility is poor but not seriously reduced. Only use your fog lights when visibility is seriously reduced. Use dipped headlights in poor conditions because this helps other road users to see you without the risk of causing dazzle.

Understand why vehicles fitted with rear fog lights. Rear fog lights make it easier to spot a vehicle ahead in foggy conditions. Avoid the temptation to use other vehicles' lights as a guide, as they may give you a false sense of security.

There is been a heavy fall of snow. Work out what should you consider before driving in these conditions. Consider whether the increased risk is worth it. Then do not drive if the weather conditions are bad and your journey is not essential. Confirm you are well prepared in case you get stuck if you have to drive.

Work out what should you check before you start a journey in foggy weather. Switch your dipped headlights on and keep all your windows clear if you have to drive in fog. Always be able to pull up within the distance you can see ahead.

You have been driving in fog. Decide what you are required to do when the visibility improves. You are required to turn off your fog lights if visibility is more than 100 metres (328 feet). Be prepared for the fact that the fog may be patchy and you may need to turn them on again if the fog returns.

Understand why it is dangerous to leave rear fog lights switched on after the fog has cleared. The glare they cause makes it difficult for road users behind to know whether you are braking or you have just forgotten to turn off your rear fog lights if your rear fog lights are left on when it is not foggy. This can be a particular problem on wet roads and on motorways. Road users behind you are likely to be dazzled and this could put them at risk if you leave your rear fog lights on at night.

Work out what will happen if you hold the clutch pedal down or roll in neutral for too long. Holding the clutch down or staying in neutral for too long will cause your vehicle to freewheel. This is known as 'coasting' and it is dangerous because it reduces your control of the vehicle.

Understand why it is bad technique to coast when you are driving downhill. Coasting is when you allow the vehicle to freewheel in neutral or with the clutch pedal depressed. This will cause the vehicle to gain speed more quickly as you lose the benefits of engine braking; it may even lead to a loss of control when travelling downhill. Do not coast, especially when approaching hazards such as junctions or bends and when travelling downhill.

Decide what to do when dealing with this hazard. In normal conditions, a ford can be crossed quite safely by driving through it slowly. The water may affect your brakes, so when you are clear of the ford, test them before you resume normal driving.

Understand why is travelling in neutral for long distances (known as coasting) bad driving technique. Try to look and plan well ahead. Plan your approach to hazards and select the correct gear in good time. This will help give you the control it is necessary to deal with anything unexpected that may occur.

Judge when you are required to use dipped headlights during the day. You are required to use dipped headlights when daytime visibility is seriously reduced, generally to 100 metres (328 feet) or less. You may also use front or rear fog lights, but they must be switched off when visibility improves.

Decide what to do when you are driving along a road that has a series of road humps. Traffic-calming measures are designed to protect vulnerable road users. Keep your speed down where traffic-calming measures are in place.

Decide what to do if you are towing a trailer and it starts to swing from side to side. Strong winds or buffeting from large vehicles can cause a trailer or caravan to swing from side to side ('snake'). Ease off the accelerator if this happens. Do not brake harshly, steer sharply or increase your speed.

Judge when you would increase the pressure in your tyres so that it is above the normal value. Check the vehicle handbook. This should give you guidance on the correct tyre pressures for your vehicle and when you may need to adjust them. You may need to adjust the headlights as well if you are carrying a heavy load. Most cars have a switch on the dashboard to do this.

Judge how a heavy load on your roof rack affect your vehicle's handling. A heavy load on your roof rack will reduce the stability of the vehicle because it moves the centre of gravity away from that designed by the manufacturer. Watch for this when you drive round bends and corners. Your vehicle and/or load could become unstable and you could lose control if you change direction at speed.

Work out what would be affected if you carry a very heavy load on your vehicle. Any load will have an effect on the handling of your vehicle, and this becomes worse as you increase the load. It is necessary to watch for this when carrying passengers or heavy loads, fitting a roof rack or towing a trailer.

Judge who is responsible for making sure that a vehicle is not overloaded. Carrying heavy loads will affect control and the vehicle's handling characteristics. You will be held responsible if the vehicle you are driving is overloaded.

You are planning to tow a caravan. Work out what will help the handling of the combination. Towing a caravan or trailer affects the way the towing vehicle handles. A stabiliser device is not designed to overcome instability caused by incorrect loading but it can give added security in side winds and from buffeting caused by large vehicles.

Decide whether passengers are allowed to ride in a caravan that is being towed. Riding in a towed caravan is highly dangerous. The safety of the entire unit is dependent on the stability of the trailer. Moving passengers would make the caravan unstable and could cause loss of control.

Work out what safety device must be fitted to a trailer braking system. In the event that the trailer becomes detached from the towing vehicle, the breakaway cable activates the trailer brakes before snapping. This allows the towing vehicle to get free of the trailer and out of danger.

You wish to tow a trailer. Judge where you would find the maximum noseweight for your vehicle's tow hitch. You are required to know how to load your trailer or caravan so that the hitch exerts an appropriate downward force on the tow ball. Information about the maximum permitted noseweight can be found in your vehicle handbook or obtained from your vehicle manufacturer's agent.

Judge how a load should be carried on your roof rack. Any load must be securely fastened to the vehicle. The safest way to carry items on the roof is in a specially designed roof box. This will help to keep your luggage secure and dry, and it also has less wind resistance than loads carried exposed on a roof rack.

You are carrying a child under 3 years old in your car. Judge which restraint is suitable for a child of this age. It is your responsibility to confirm that all children under 14 years old in your car are secure. Suitable restraints include a child seat, baby seat, booster seat or booster cushion. It is essential that any restraint used is suitable for the child's size and weight, and fitted according to the manufacturer's instructions.

You have just passed your driving test. Work out the maximum authorised mass (MAM) of any trailer that you can tow. You are allowed to tow a trailer up to 3,500 kg MAM without taking an extra test when you pass your driving test. You will have to pass either a CE or DE category test, dependent on the towing vehicle if you want to tow a heavier trailer.

Decide what to do before you tow a trailer for the first time. It is necessary to know how to tow a trailer safely. This includes hitching the trailer to your vehicle, checking the trailer for defects, reversing with a trailer and how to deal with any problems. There are accredited trainers who can teach you these skills. Professional training will also give you confidence in your ability to tow a trailer safely.

You are going to tow a trailer that is wider than your car. Work out what you are required to fit to your car before you start towing it. You are required to fit exterior towing mirrors to your vehicle if • your vehicle is narrower than your trailer or load • your trailer or load obstructs the view behind you.

Decide what you are required to do when you hitch an unbraked trailer to a towing vehicle. The trailer must stay connected to the towing vehicle if a tow hitch fails. This is achieved by using a secondary coupling device, such as a safety chain.

Work out the minimum depth of tread on the tyres of a trailer. Your car or small van must have a minimum tread depth of 1.6 mm across the centre of the tread and around the entire circumference. This also applies to the tyres on your trailer.

You are about to start a journey towing a trailer. Decide what to do if you notice that a light on your trailer is not working. You are required to confirm that your vehicle and trailer are roadworthy. Check that your tyres are legal, and the brakes and lights are working properly. Do not drive or tow your trailer until the fault is repaired if any of these things are not working.

Work out what it means if your trailer has a maximum authorised mass (MAM) of 3,500 kg. The MAM of the trailer is stamped on the plate fitted to the chassis. It is the maximum weight of the trailer and load that the manufacturer has designed it to carry. Do not load your trailer so that it exceeds this maximum weight.
Decide what to do if your trailer starts to swerve or snake. Reduce speed gently to regain control if your trailer starts to swerve or snake. Do not accelerate or brake harshly.

Judge how you should load your trailer. The safe action is to spread the weight evenly with heavy items over the axles when loading your trailer. This should reduce the risk of it swerving or snaking.

Judge when you may overtake another vehicle on their left. You may pass slower vehicles on their left while travelling along a one-way street. Watch for drivers who may need to change lanes and may not expect faster traffic passing on their left.

You are travelling in very heavy rain. Keep this situation in mind: how is this likely to affect your overall stopping distance. The road will be very wet and spray from other vehicles will reduce your visibility. Tyre grip will also be reduced, increasing your stopping distance. The safe action is to at least double your separation distance to confirm you can stop safely in the space you have allowed.

Decide what to do when you are overtaking at night. Do not overtake if there is a possibility of a road junction, bend or brow of a bridge or hill ahead. There are many hazards that are difficult to see in the dark. Only overtake if you are certain that the road ahead is clear. Do not take a chance.

Judge when you may wait in a box junction. The purpose of a box junction is to keep the junction clear by preventing vehicles from stopping in the path of crossing traffic. Do not enter a box junction unless your exit is clear. However, you may enter the box and wait if you want to turn right and are only prevented from doing so by oncoming traffic.

Work out the reason for traffic-calming measures. Traffic-calming measures make the roads safer for vulnerable road users, such as cyclists, pedestrians and children. These can be designed as chicanes, road humps or other obstacles that encourage drivers and riders to slow down.

Work out what colour are the reflective studs along the left-hand edge of the motorway. Reflective studs are used to help you in poor visibility. Different colours are used so that you will know which lane you are in. These are • red on the left-hand edge of the carriageway • white between lanes • amber on the right-hand edge of the carriageway • green between the carriageway and slip roads.

Decide what to do if you have to make a journey in foggy conditions. Listen to the weather reports if you are planning to make a journey when it is foggy. Avoid making unnecessary journeys if visibility is very poor. Leave plenty of time – and if someone is waiting for you to arrive, let them know that your journey will take longer than normal if you do travel. This will also take off any pressure you may feel to rush.

Decide what you are required to do when you are overtaking a car at night. To prevent your headlights from dazzling the driver of the car in front, wait until you have passed them before switching to main beam.

You are travelling on a road that has road humps. Decide what to do when the driver in front is travelling more slowly than you. Be patient and stay behind the car in front. Do not normally overtake other vehicles in areas subject to traffic calming. You may easily exceed the speed limit, defeating the purpose of the traffic-calming measures if you overtake here.

Decide what to do when you meet an oncoming vehicle on a single-track road. Take care when using single-track roads. It can be difficult to see around bends, because of hedges or fences, so expect to meet oncoming vehicles. Drive carefully and be ready to pull into or stop opposite a passing place, where you can pass each other safely.

The road is wet. Understand why would a motorcyclist steer around drain covers while they were cornering. Other drivers or riders may have to change course due to the size or characteristics of their vehicle. Understanding this will help you to anticipate their actions. Motorcyclists and cyclists will be checking the road ahead for uneven or slippery surfaces, especially in wet weather. They may need to move across their lane to avoid surface hazards such as potholes and drain covers.

Understand why you should test your brakes after this hazard. A ford is a crossing over a stream that is shallow enough to drive or ride through. Your brakes will be wet and they will not work as well as usual after you have gone through a ford or deep puddle. To dry them out, apply a light brake pressure while moving slowly. Do not travel at normal speeds until you are sure your brakes are working properly again.

Understand why you should reduce your speed when you are driving or riding in fog. You will not be able to see as far ahead in fog as you can on a clear day. You will need to reduce your speed so that, if a hazard looms out of the fog, you have the time and space to take avoiding action. Travelling in fog is hazardous. Try to delay your journey until it has cleared if you can.

Work out what restrictions apply if you are towing a trailer on a three-lane motorway. The motorway regulations for towing a trailer state that do not • use the right-hand lane of a three-lane motorway unless directed to do so (for instance, at roadworks or due to a lane closure) • exceed 60 mph.

You are turning right from a main road into a side road. There is no oncoming traffic. Decide what to do if pedestrians are standing on the pavement waiting to cross the side road. The safe action is to give way to pedestrians crossing or waiting to cross the road into which or from which you are turning. Be patient if they are cautious and take their time checking that it is safe before they step into the road.

You are travelling on a narrow section of road. Decide what to do if a horse rider ahead is riding in the centre of the lane. On narrow sections of road, horse riders may ride in the centre of the lane. This is for their own safety as it makes them more visible. The safe action is to be patient and only pass when it is safe to do so.

You are about to overtake a cyclist on a road that has a 30 mph speed limit. Keep this situation in mind: how much room should you leave them as you overtake. The safe action is to leave cyclists at least as much room as you would if you were overtaking a car. Leave them more room if you are overtaking at speeds over 30 mph.

You are turning left from a main road into a side road. Decide what to do if there is a pedestrian on the pavement waiting to cross the side road. The safe action is to give way to pedestrians crossing or waiting to cross the road into which or from which you are turning. Be patient if they are cautious, and let them check that it is safe from all directions before they step into the road. Do not signal or wave them to cross.

Decide what to do if you want to turn left at a junction where pedestrians have started to cross. Pedestrians who are crossing have priority when you are turning into a side road. The safe action is to wait to allow them to finish crossing safely. Be patient if they are slow or unsteady. Do not try to rush them by sounding your horn, flashing your lights, revving your engine or giving any other inappropriate signal.

Work out what hazard should you be especially aware of if you are turning left into a side road. Confirm that you have reduced your speed and are in the correct gear for the turn. Look into the road before you turn and always give way to any pedestrians who are crossing.

Understand why you should check for motorcyclists just before turning right into a side road. Never attempt to change direction to the right without first checking your right-hand mirror and blind spot. A motorcyclist might not have seen your signal and could be hidden by other traffic. This observation should be routine.

Understand how a toucan crossing is different from a puffin crossing. Puffin crossings are for use by pedestrians. Cyclists must dismount and push their bicycle over the crossing. Toucan crossings are shared by pedestrians and cyclists, who are permitted to cycle over the crossing. Toucan roadside signals show an icon of a pedestrian and a cyclist together.

Judge how a school crossing patrol signal you to stop. You are required to stop if a school crossing patrol steps out into the road with a 'stop' sign. Do not wave anyone across the road and do not get impatient or rev your engine.

You see a pedestrian carrying a white stick that also has a red band. Work out what this mean. They may carry a white stick with a red reflective band or bands when someone is deaf as well as blind. They may not stay alert that you are approaching and they may not be able to hear anything; so, for instance, your horn would be ineffective as a warning to them.

Decide what you would do if you see older people crossing the road ahead. Stay alert that older people might take a long time to cross the road. They might also be hard of hearing and not hear you approaching. Do not hurry older people across the road by getting too close to them or revving your engine.

Decide what to do when you see an older person about to cross the road ahead. Older people may have impaired hearing, vision, concentration and judgement. They may also walk slowly and so could take a long time to cross the road.

You are approaching a roundabout. Decide what to do if a cyclist ahead is signalling to turn right. Leave plenty of room if you are following a cyclist who is signalling to turn right at a roundabout. Give them space and time to get into the correct lane.

Judge which vehicle should you allow extra room as you overtake them. Do not pass cyclists too closely, as they may • need to veer around a pothole, drain or other hazard • be buffeted by side wind • be made unsteady by your vehicle. Always leave as much room as you would for a car, and do not cut in front of them.

Understand why you should look carefully for motorcyclists and cyclists at junctions. Cyclists and motorcyclists are smaller than other vehicles and so are more difficult to see. They can easily be hidden from your view by cars parked near a junction.

You are waiting to come out of a side road. Understand why you should look carefully for motorcycles. Look carefully for motorcycles: they can be difficult to see if you are waiting to emerge from a side road.
