Be especially careful if there are parked vehicles or other obstructions restricting your view.

Understand why do motorcyclists use dipped headlights in daylight. A motorcycle can be lost from sight behind another vehicle. The use of headlights helps to make it more conspicuous and therefore more easily seen.

Understand why do motorcyclists wear bright clothing. Motorcycles and mopeds are generally smaller than other vehicles and can be difficult to see. Wearing bright clothing makes it easier for other road users to see a motorcyclist approaching, especially at junctions.

Understand why do motorcyclists often look round over their right shoulder just before turning right. They are probably about to change direction when you see a motorcyclist take a glance over their shoulder. Recognising a clue like this helps you to anticipate their next action. This can improve road safety for you and others.

Judge which is the most vulnerable road user. Pedestrians and riders on 2 wheels can be harder to see than other road users. Confirm you look for them, especially at junctions. Effective observation, coupled with appropriate action, can save lives.

You are approaching a roundabout. Decide what to do if there are horses being ridden in front of you. Horse riders often keep to the outside of the roundabout even if they are turning right. Give them plenty of room and remember that they may have to cross lanes of traffic.

As you approach a pelican crossing, the lights change to green. Decide what to do if older people are still crossing. Wait for any pedestrians to clear the crossing if the lights turn to green. Allow them to finish crossing the road in their own time, and do not try to hurry them by revving your engine.

Decide what action you should take when you see flashing amber lights under a school warning sign. The flashing amber lights are switched on to warn you that children may be crossing near a school. Slow down and take extra care, as you may have to stop.

Understand why should these road markings be kept clear. The markings are there to show that the area should be kept clear. This is to allow an unrestricted view for • approaching drivers and riders • children wanting to cross the road.

You are following 2 cyclists as they approach a roundabout in the left-hand lane. Judge where you would expect the cyclists to go. Cyclists approaching a roundabout in the left-hand lane may be turning right but may not have been able to get into the correct lane due to heavy traffic. They may also feel safer keeping to the left all the way around the roundabout. Watch for them and give them plenty of room.

You are travelling behind a moped. Decide what to do if you want to turn left a short distance ahead. Passing the moped and turning into the junction could mean that you cut across the front of the rider. This might force them to slow down, stop or even lose control. Stay behind the moped until it has passed the junction and then you can turn without affecting the rider.

You see a horse rider as you approach a roundabout. Decide what to do if they are signalling right but keeping well to the left. Allow the horse rider to enter and exit the roundabout in their own time. They may feel safer keeping to the left all the way around the roundabout. Do not get up close behind or alongside them, because that would probably upset the horse and create a dangerous situation.

Judge how you should react to inexperienced drivers. Learners might not have confidence when they first start to drive. Allow them plenty of room and do not react adversely to their hesitation. We all learn from experience, but new drivers will have had less practice in dealing with all the situations that might occur.

Decide what to do when you are following a learner driver who stalls at a junction. Learning to drive is a process of practice and experience. Try to understand this and tolerate those who make mistakes while they are learning.

You are on a country road. Work out what should you expect to see coming towards you on your side of the road. On a quiet country road, always stay alert that there may be a hazard just around the next bend, such as a slow-moving vehicle or pedestrians. Pedestrians are advised to walk on the right-hand side of the road if there is no pavement, so they may be walking towards you on your side of the road.

You are following a cyclist. Decide what to do when you wish to turn left a short distance ahead. Make allowances for cyclists, and give them plenty of room. Do not overtake and then immediately turn left. Be patient and turn behind them when they have passed the junction.

A horse rider is in the left-hand lane approaching a roundabout. Judge where you should expect the rider to go. Horses and their riders move more slowly than other road users. They might not have time to cut across heavy traffic to take up a position in the right-hand lane. For this reason, a horse and rider may approach a roundabout in the left-hand lane even though they are turning right.

Powered vehicles used by disabled people are small and can be hard to see. Work out what must they display if they are travelling on a dual carriageway. Powered vehicles used by disabled people are small and low making them hard to see on the road. They also travel very slowly. On an unrestricted dual carriageway, they must display a flashing amber beacon to warn other road users of their presence.

Work out what it means when a moving vehicle is showing a flashing amber beacon. Different coloured beacons warn of different types of vehicle needing special attention. Blue beacons are used on emergency vehicles that need priority. Green beacons are found on doctors' cars. Amber beacons generally denote slower moving vehicles, which are often large. These vehicles are usually involved in road maintenance or local amenities and make frequent stops.

Decide what to do when you see these horse riders in front. Be particularly careful when approaching horse riders – slow down and be prepared to stop. Always pass wide and slowly, and look out for signals given by the riders. Horses are unpredictable: always treat them as potential hazards and take great care when passing them.

Work out the purpose of these road markings. These markings are found on the road outside schools. Do not stop or park on them, even to set down or pick up children. The markings are there to confirm that drivers, riders, children and other pedestrians have a clear view of the road in all directions.

Decide what to do if the left-hand pavement is closed due to street repairs. Where street repairs have closed off pavements, proceed carefully and slowly, as pedestrians might have to walk in the road.

Decide what to do when you are following a motorcyclist along a road that has a poor surface. To avoid being unbalanced, a motorcyclist might swerve to avoid potholes and bumps in the road. Be prepared for this and allow them extra space.

You are approaching this roundabout. Decide what to do when a cyclist is keeping to the left while signalling to turn right. Cycling in today's heavy traffic can be hazardous. Some cyclists may not feel safe crossing the path of traffic to take up a position in an outside lane. Watch for this and understand that, although they are in the left-hand lane, the cyclist might be turning right.
Decide what to do when you are approaching this crossing. Be courteous and prepare to stop. Do not wave people across, because this could be dangerous if another vehicle is approaching the crossing.

Work out what it means if you see a pedestrian with a dog that has a yellow or burgundy coat. Dogs trained to help deaf people have a yellow or burgundy coat. The safe action is to take extra care, as the pedestrian may not watch for vehicles approaching if you see one.

Judge who may use toucan crossings. There are some crossings where cycle routes lead cyclists to cross at the same place as pedestrians. These are called toucan crossings. Always look out for cyclists, as they are likely to be approaching faster than pedestrians.

This junction, controlled by traffic lights, has a marked area between 2 stop lines. Work out this for. These are known as advanced stop lines. The safe action is to stop at the first white line when the lights are red (or about to become red). However, if you have crossed that line as the lights change, you are required to stop at the second line even if it means you are in the area reserved for cyclists.

You are about to overtake a cyclist. Understand why you should leave them as much room as you would give to a car. Assess the situation before overtaking. Look well ahead to see whether the cyclist will need to change direction. Be especially aware of a cyclist approaching parked vehicles, as they will need to alter course. Do not pass too closely or cut in sharply as this could unsettle the rider.

Decide what to do when you are passing loose sheep on the road. Slow down and be ready to stop if you see animals in the road ahead. Animals are easily frightened by noise and vehicles passing too close to them. Stop if you are signalled to do so by the person in charge.

At night, work out what it means if you see a pedestrian wearing reflective clothing and carrying a bright red light. The people on the walk should be keeping to the left, but do not assume this. Pass carefully, making sure you have time to do so safely. Stay alert that the pedestrians have their backs to you and may not know that you are there.

You have just passed your driving or riding test. Judge how you can reduce your risk of being involved in a collision. New drivers and riders are often involved in a collision or incident early in their driving career. Due to a lack of experience, they may not react to hazards appropriately. Approved training courses are offered by driver and rider training schools for people who have passed their test but want extra training.

You want to reverse into a side road. Decide what to do if you are not sure that the area behind your car is clear. It is always safest to check before reversing if you cannot tell whether there is anything behind you. There may be a small child or a low obstruction close behind your car.

You are about to reverse into a side road. Decide what to do if a pedestrian is waiting to cross behind your car. Try to find a place that is free from traffic and pedestrians if it is necessary to reverse into a side road. Look all around before and during the manoeuvre. Stop and give way to any pedestrians who want to cross behind you. Avoid waving them across, sounding the horn, flashing your lights or giving any signals that could mislead them and create a dangerous situation.

Judge which road users are most difficult to see when you are reversing your car. It may not be possible to see a small child through the rear windscreen of your vehicle. Watch for this before you reverse. Get out and check that it is clear before reversing if there are children about.

You want to turn right from a junction. Decide what to do if your view is restricted by parked vehicles. Stop if you want to turn right from a junction and your view is restricted. Ease forward until you can see – something might be approaching. Do not go if you do not know.

You are at the front of a queue of traffic waiting to turn right into a side road. Understand why it is important to check your right mirror just before turning. A motorcyclist could be riding along the outside of the queue. Always check your mirror before turning, as situations behind you can change while you have been waiting to turn.

You have driven up to a pelican crossing. Decide what you are required to do while the amber light is flashing. The flashing amber light allows pedestrians already on the crossing to get to the other side before a green light shows to the traffic. Stay alert that some pedestrians, such as older people and young children, need longer to cross. Let them do this at their own pace.

You have stopped at a pelican crossing. Decide what to do if a disabled person is crossing slowly in front of you and the lights change to green. At a pelican crossing, the green light means you may proceed as long as the crossing is clear. Be patient and wait for them, whether they are disabled or not if someone has not finished crossing.

You are driving past a line of parked cars. Decide what to do if a ball bounces out into the road ahead. Beware of children playing in the street and running out into the road. Slow down and be prepared to stop if a ball bounces out from the pavement. Do not encourage anyone to retrieve it. Other road users may not see your signal and you might lead a child into a dangerous situation.

You want to turn right from a main road into a side road. Decide what to do just before turning. In some circumstances, your indicators may be difficult to see and another road user may not realise you are about to turn. A final check in your mirror and blind spot can help you to see an overtaking vehicle, so that you can avoid turning across their path.

You are driving in a slow-moving queue of traffic. Decide what to do just before changing lane. In queuing traffic, motorcyclists could be passing you on either side. Use your mirrors and check your blind area before changing lanes or changing direction.

You are driving in town. Understand why you should be careful if there is a bus at a bus stop on the other side of the road. Watch out for pedestrians if you see a bus ahead. They might not be able to see you if they are behind the bus.

Judge how you should overtake horse riders. Confirm you can do so safely before you move out when you decide to overtake a horse rider. Leave them plenty of room and pass slowly. Passing too close could startle the horse and unseat the rider.

Understand why you should allow extra room while overtaking a motorcyclist on a windy day. Stay alert that the conditions might make a motorcyclist (or cyclist) swerve or wobble if you are driving in high winds. Take this into consideration if you are following or wish to overtake a two-wheeled vehicle.

Judge where you should take particular care to look for motorcyclists and cyclists. Motorcyclists and cyclists are often more difficult to see at junctions. They are easily hidden from view and you may not be able to see them approaching a junction if your view is partially blocked; for instance, by other traffic.

The road outside this school is marked with yellow zigzag lines. Work out what do these lines mean. Parking here would block other road users' view of the school entrance and would endanger the lives of children on their way to and from school.

You are driving past parked cars. Decide what to do if you see a bicycle wheel sticking out between the cars. Scan the road as you drive. Try to anticipate hazards by being aware of the places where they are likely to occur. You will then be able to react in good time.

You are driving at night. Decide what to do if you are dazzled by a vehicle behind you. The interior mirror of most vehicles can be set to an anti-dazzle position. You will still be able to see the lights of the traffic behind you, but the dazzle will be greatly reduced.

You are driving towards a zebra crossing. Decide what to do if a person in a wheelchair is waiting to cross. The safe action is to slow down and be prepared to stop, as you would for an able-bodied person. Do not wave them across, as other traffic may not stop.
